title: Polarization Around the Character of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib
author: Ayatullah Murtadha Mutahhari

units.title: Preface & Foreword

chunks.title: 'Ali's personality is too vast for any one person to treat completely; a writer must choose one limited aspect
chunks.text: 'Ali's personality is too vast for any one person to treat completely; a writer must choose one limited aspect. Mutahhari chooses his attraction and repulsion.

chunks.title: The weaker a personality, the fewer minds it engages
chunks.text: The weaker a personality, the fewer minds it engages. The greater it is, the more it provokes reaction — positive or negative. Great personalities become subjects of debate, poetry, painting, story.

chunks.title: What distinguishes 'Ali (and others lit by Truth) is that they don't only engage the mind — they give light, warmth, love, joy, faith and st
chunks.text: What distinguishes 'Ali (and others lit by Truth) is that they don't only engage the mind — they give light, warmth, love, joy, faith and strength to hearts.

chunks.title: The three rival types and their limits: philosophers produce students, not followers; social leaders create followers but not complete men;
chunks.text: The three rival types and their limits: philosophers produce students, not followers; social leaders create followers but not complete men; Sufi shaykhs make 'lords of submission', not active fighters. 'Ali combines all four schools — intellect, revolution, submission/discipline, and beauty/ecstasy.

chunks.title: Before being a just leader of others, 'Ali was himself a harmonized, equilibrated being — night in worship, day active among people; both le
chunks.text: Before being a just leader of others, 'Ali was himself a harmonized, equilibrated being — night in worship, day active among people; both learned and wise, both gnostic and social leader, both judge and worker.

chunks.title: Mutahhari's self-critical thesis in the Foreword: how often have we who claim to follow 'Ali pushed away the very people 'Ali attracted, and
chunks.text: Mutahhari's self-critical thesis in the Foreword: how often have we who claim to follow 'Ali pushed away the very people 'Ali attracted, and attracted those he repelled?

chunks.title: He admits a deficiency: in the repulsion section he treats only the Khawarij, though other groups were also repelled — he hopes to amend thi
chunks.text: He admits a deficiency: in the repulsion section he treats only the Khawarij, though other groups were also repelled — he hopes to amend this in a future printing.

akhlaq.lesson: Treat intellectual and spiritual influence as a responsibility: cultivate the character that makes your teaching or leadership worth following, not merely admired.

units.title: The Law of Attraction and Repulsion

chunks.title: Attraction is a universal law of creation, not a metaphor: from the largest masses to the smallest atoms, nothing escapes general attraction
chunks.text: Attraction is a universal law of creation, not a metaphor: from the largest masses to the smallest atoms, nothing escapes general attraction.

chunks.title: Ancient man knew only particular attractions — magnet/iron, amber/straw — not the universal law behind them.
chunks.text: Ancient man knew only particular attractions — magnet/iron, amber/straw — not the universal law behind them.

chunks.title: Old cosmology: why does the earth stay fixed? Some said it is attracted equally from every side; others said the heavens repel it equally fr
chunks.text: Old cosmology: why does the earth stay fixed? Some said it is attracted equally from every side; others said the heavens repel it equally from every side. Either way, equilibrium.

chunks.title: Ancient physiology applied the same idea to living things: plants/animals have nutritive, growth, and reproductive faculties; the nutritive
chunks.text: Ancient physiology applied the same idea to living things: plants/animals have nutritive, growth, and reproductive faculties; the nutritive faculty subdivides into attractive, repulsive, digestive, retentive. The stomach 'draws in' food; the liver 'draws in' water.

chunks.title: A footnote flags the contrast with electricity: like poles repel, unlike poles attract — the reverse of the human case, where resemblance at
chunks.text: A footnote flags the contrast with electricity: like poles repel, unlike poles attract — the reverse of the human case, where resemblance attracts.

akhlaq.lesson: Notice attraction and repulsion as structural forces in life, and use them deliberately rather than assuming every relationship should be frictionless.

units.title: Attraction and Repulsion in the World of Man

chunks.title: Scope limit: this is NOT about sexual attraction (a separate enquiry), and NOT about cooperation based on shared material benefit
chunks.text: Scope limit: this is NOT about sexual attraction (a separate enquiry), and NOT about cooperation based on shared material benefit. It is about friendship, affection, enmity and hatred in social life.

chunks.title: The root cause is general resemblance (similarity) or contrariety (tadadd)
chunks.text: The root cause is general resemblance (similarity) or contrariety (tadadd). Metaphysics has proved that general resemblance is the cause of union.

chunks.title: No two people become friends without a reason; no two become enemies without a cause
chunks.text: No two people become friends without a reason; no two become enemies without a cause. Closeness is itself evidence of some hidden similarity.

chunks.title: The rival theory — need: man is created essentially in want
chunks.text: The rival theory — need: man is created essentially in want. He is drawn to whoever fills his emptiness, repelled by whoever adds to it, and indifferent to whoever does neither. All inclination springs from the instinct for taking advantage.

chunks.title: Either way: attraction and repulsion are two fundamental pillars of human life
chunks.text: Either way: attraction and repulsion are two fundamental pillars of human life. Reduce them and disorder replaces order.

akhlaq.lesson: Judge friendship and hostility by the qualities they reveal: similarity, difference, benefit, principle, and character—not by surface popularity alone.

units.title: Differences Between People — The Four Types

chunks.title: Type 1 — attracts nothing, repels nothing
chunks.text: Type 1 — attracts nothing, repels nothing. Nobody's friend, nobody's enemy. Goes among men 'just as if a slab of rock were to be among them'. Produces no effect, positive or negative — and 'positive' here covers wickedness as well as virtue. Compared to a sheep, fed only because its meat will be eaten. Man needs to love and be loved, and also to hate and be hated. Verdict: hollow, vacuous, worthless.

chunks.title: Type 2 — attracts all, repels none
chunks.text: Type 2 — attracts all, repels none. The Zamzam/cremation poem: live so Muslims wash you with Zamzam water and Hindus cremate you. Often mistaken for 'good character' or 'being sociable'. But impossible for anyone with a real aim, unless he is a hypocrite and double-faced. Men do not all think alike — there are just and unjust, equitable and despotic. Only the dissimulator pleases everyone.

chunks.title: Critique of 'love-only' philosophies: some Christians and Hindus hold the perfect man has only attraction
chunks.text: Critique of 'love-only' philosophies: some Christians and Hindus hold the perfect man has only attraction. Mutahhari: it is not enough to be a man of love, one must be a man with a path — as Gandhi said, 'This is my religion.' Love must coincide with reality; reality has a path; a path creates enemies.

chunks.title: Qur'anic balance: the Prophet is rahmatan li'l-'alamin (21:107) — mercy to all beings, even the dangerous enemy
chunks.text: Qur'anic balance: the Prophet is rahmatan li'l-'alamin (21:107) — mercy to all beings, even the dangerous enemy. But love does not mean approving everyone's inclinations; that is hypocrisy. Rational love seeks the good of mankind as a whole, not one individual or group — and many things that benefit an individual harm society.

chunks.title: Ibn Muljam: 'Ali knew he was a dangerous enemy; others urged him to act
chunks.text: Ibn Muljam: 'Ali knew he was a dangerous enemy; others urged him to act. 'Should I punish before the crime? He is to murder me, not I him.' — I want him to live; he wants to kill me.

chunks.title: Type 3 — repels all, attracts none
chunks.text: Type 3 — repels all, attracts none. Also deficient: since there are always some good people, a man with no friends must have the fault in himself. Such people are 'sour throughout', even in their villainy.

chunks.title: Type 4 — attracts AND repels
chunks.text: Type 4 — attracts AND repels. People travelling a path. Strength varies: at maximum, friends give their souls and enemies give their lives, and the effect persists centuries after death. But — crucially — this is not proof of virtue. Genghis Khan, Hajjaj and Mu'awiyah all had both powers strongly. What matters is who is attracted and who repelled: these are 'a clear proof of the essence of such a person'.

chunks.title: Nadir Shah (b
chunks.text: Nadir Shah (b. 1688, r. 1736, d. 1747): gouged eyes and cut off heads, yet rebuilt an army from a defeated post-Safavid Iran 'just like a magnet that attracts iron-filings'.

chunks.title: Newtonian analogy: pull increases with the mass of the body and decreases with distance — so too among men.
chunks.text: Newtonian analogy: pull increases with the mass of the body and decreases with distance — so too among men.

akhlaq.lesson: Do not confuse universal popularity with virtue. A principled person may attract some people and repel others; examine whom your character draws and why.

units.title: 'Ali — One Man with Two Powers

chunks.title: 'Ali's attraction and repulsion are arguably unmatched in any century or epoch.
chunks.text: 'Ali's attraction and repulsion are arguably unmatched in any century or epoch.

chunks.title: His friends were 'truly historical persons' — self-sacrificing, forbearing, 'burning with love for him like flames from a bonfire'
chunks.text: His friends were 'truly historical persons' — self-sacrificing, forbearing, 'burning with love for him like flames from a bonfire'. They made giving their lives their aim and glory.

chunks.title: After his death, under Mu'awiyah and the Umayyads, masses were arrested for the crime of friendship to him and tortured, yet did not give wa
chunks.text: After his death, under Mu'awiyah and the Umayyads, masses were arrested for the crime of friendship to him and tortured, yet did not give way.

chunks.title: Ordinary men die and are covered by earth; men of truth die but their following grows more brilliant with the centuries.
chunks.text: Ordinary men die and are covered by earth; men of truth die but their following grows more brilliant with the centuries.

chunks.title: Maytham at-Tammar: twenty years after 'Ali's martyrdom, when all freedoms were quashed and 'a mortal silence showed like the mist of death o
chunks.text: Maytham at-Tammar: twenty years after 'Ali's martyrdom, when all freedoms were quashed and 'a mortal silence showed like the mist of death on everyone's faces', he preached 'Ali's virtues from his own crucifix. Crowds thronged; the Umayyad government ordered a gag put in his mouth and days later ended his life.

chunks.title: Ibn as-Sikkit: a giant of Arabic letters, ranked with Sibawayh, living under al-Mutawakkil ~200 years after 'Ali
chunks.text: Ibn as-Sikkit: a giant of Arabic letters, ranked with Sibawayh, living under al-Mutawakkil ~200 years after 'Ali. Accused of Shi'ism yet appointed tutor to the caliph's sons. Asked whether the caliph's two sons were dearer to him than Hasan and Husayn, he answered that 'Ali's slave Qanbar was dearer than these two and their father. His tongue was cut out from his throat.

chunks.title: Key interpretive move: ''Ali is not to be looked at as an individual, but rather as a whole philosophy' — which is why one group is attracte
chunks.text: Key interpretive move: ''Ali is not to be looked at as an individual, but rather as a whole philosophy' — which is why one group is attracted and one repelled.

akhlaq.lesson: Seek the balance of attraction and repulsion: welcome people toward truth while remaining firm enough to resist falsehood, corruption, and injustice.

units.title: Powerful Attractions (Part 1 opens)

chunks.title: From the introduction to The Seal of the Prophets (Khatim-e Payambaran), on 'calls' to mankind:
chunks.text: From the introduction to The Seal of the Prophets (Khatim-e Payambaran), on 'calls' to mankind:

chunks.title: One-dimensional: embrace millions, then 'close shop and are entrusted to oblivion'.
chunks.text: One-dimensional: embrace millions, then 'close shop and are entrusted to oblivion'.

chunks.title: Two-dimensional: broad and extend into the temporal dimension — they last.
chunks.text: Two-dimensional: broad and extend into the temporal dimension — they last.

chunks.title: Three-dimensional: broad, temporal, and they 'take root in the depths of the human spirit… rule in the profundity of the soul and take the r
chunks.text: Three-dimensional: broad, temporal, and they 'take root in the depths of the human spirit… rule in the profundity of the soul and take the reins of the emotions'. This kind is the exclusivity of the chain of the prophets.

chunks.title: Rhetorical challenge: what philosophical school rules hundreds of millions for thirty, twenty, or at minimum fourteen centuries and sinks in
chunks.text: Rhetorical challenge: what philosophical school rules hundreds of millions for thirty, twenty, or at minimum fourteen centuries and sinks into their innermost core?

chunks.title: 'Ali's attraction is of the third kind — after hundreds of years, hearing his virtues still draws tears of longing, 'to the extent that even
chunks.text: 'Ali's attraction is of the third kind — after hundreds of years, hearing his virtues still draws tears of longing, 'to the extent that even his enemies are affected and their tears flow'.

chunks.title: Therefore the link between man and religion is not material but of another kind entirely.
chunks.text: Therefore the link between man and religion is not material but of another kind entirely.

chunks.title: The counterfactual: had 'Ali lacked divine colouring and not been a man of God, he would have been forgotten — like all the champions of spe
chunks.text: The counterfactual: had 'Ali lacked divine colouring and not been a man of God, he would have been forgotten — like all the champions of speech, knowledge, philosophy, power and the battlefield who are now forgotten or unknown. Instead, 'not only did 'Ali not die with his being killed, he became more alive'.

chunks.title: Iqbal's poem is quoted at length ('My own age does not understand my deep meanings… Many a poet was born after his death').
chunks.text: Iqbal's poem is quoted at length ('My own age does not understand my deep meanings… Many a poet was born after his death').

chunks.title: Kahlil Gibran: 'Ali was one of those personalities born before his time.
chunks.text: Kahlil Gibran: 'Ali was one of those personalities born before his time.

akhlaq.lesson: Let love for a worthy model become transformative: admiration should produce imitation, discipline, courage, and concrete change rather than sentiment alone.

units.title: Shi'ism, the Creed of Love

chunks.title: The greatest mark of distinction of Shi'ism over other sects is that its foundation and bedrock is love — present from the Prophet's own tim
chunks.text: The greatest mark of distinction of Shi'ism over other sects is that its foundation and bedrock is love — present from the Prophet's own time.

chunks.title: 'Aliyyun wa shi'atuhu humu 'l-fa'izun — ''Ali and his party (Shi'ah) will be the triumphant ones.' Footnote is important: as-Suyuti relates
chunks.text: 'Aliyyun wa shi'atuhu humu 'l-fa'izun — ''Ali and his party (Shi'ah) will be the triumphant ones.' Footnote is important: as-Suyuti relates it in ad-Durr al-manthur under Surah al-Bayyinah v.7, from Ibn 'Asakir, from Jabir ibn 'Abdillah al-Ansari; also al-Manawi, al-Haythami, and Ibn Hajar in as-Sawa'iq al-muhriqah — i.e. Sunni sources.

chunks.title: Taking 'Ali as one's friend is the way of love
chunks.text: Taking 'Ali as one's friend is the way of love. Shi'ism's history is joined with 'a chain of entirely unknown people, devoted, full of love and self-sacrificing'.

chunks.title: The paradox: 'Ali applied the hudud — lashes, even amputation — and those punished did not turn away; their love did not diminish in the sli
chunks.text: The paradox: 'Ali applied the hudud — lashes, even amputation — and those punished did not turn away; their love did not diminish in the slightest.

chunks.title: 'Ali's explanation: strike a believer with this sword and it will not create enmity; pour the whole world on a hypocrite's head and he will
chunks.text: 'Ali's explanation: strike a believer with this sword and it will not create enmity; pour the whole world on a hypocrite's head and he will never love you. Decreed by the Prophet's tongue.

chunks.title: Therefore 'Ali is the standard and criterion (mi'yar) for assaying human natures
chunks.text: Therefore 'Ali is the standard and criterion (mi'yar) for assaying human natures. A sound nature never takes offence at 'Ali even under his sword; a diseased nature never attaches to him even after great favours — 'for 'Ali is nothing but the embodiment of truth'.

chunks.title: The amputation story: a good believing man fell into error and had the fingers of his right hand cut off
chunks.text: The amputation story: a good believing man fell into error and had the fingers of his right hand cut off. Holding the bleeding hand in his left, he walked away. Ibn al-Kawwa', a seditious Kharijite, approached 'with an air of utter compassion' to exploit it politically: 'Who cut your hand off?' The man answered with a sustained eulogy — chief of the Prophet's successors, leader of the untainted at the Resurrection, most righteous of believers, Imam of right guidance, first to reach the Gardens of Felicity, hero of the brave, giver of zakat, champion of Mecca. Ibn al-Kawwa': 'Poor you! He cut off your hand and you extol him thus!'

akhlaq.lesson: Make love a form of allegiance to truth and goodness, not merely affection for a personality or group identity.

units.title: The Elixir of Love

chunks.title: Persian poets called love the iksir (elixir) / kimiya (philosopher's stone) — the alchemists' substance that transmutes one matter into anot
chunks.text: Persian poets called love the iksir (elixir) / kimiya (philosopher's stone) — the alchemists' substance that transmutes one matter into another. Footnote: Burhan-e Qati' defines elixir as what melts down, combines, and perfects — and love has all three properties, though the famous sense is the third. Hence poets also call love 'the doctor', 'the drug', 'Plato', 'Galen'.

chunks.title: al-Nasu ma'adin ka-ma'adin al-dhahab wa'l-fiddah — 'People are mines, like gold-mines and silver-mines.' Different natures; love is what tra
chunks.text: al-Nasu ma'adin ka-ma'adin al-dhahab wa'l-fiddah — 'People are mines, like gold-mines and silver-mines.' Different natures; love is what transmutes them.

chunks.title: Effect 1 — power/courage
chunks.text: Effect 1 — power/courage. The hen: alone she folds her wings, pecks for worms, startles at any noise, won't face the weakest child. Give her chicks and her character completely changes — wings lowered in defensive readiness, aggressive posture, clucking stronger, and she now attacks where she formerly fled.

chunks.title: Effect 2 — diligence/wit
chunks.text: Effect 2 — diligence/wit. A boy and girl who thought only of themselves become concerned for another being; the radius of their wants extends. The lazy adolescent becomes active; the girl who wouldn't leave her bedclothes 'moves like lightning' at her child's cry.

chunks.title: Effect 3 — generosity/endurance
chunks.text: Effect 3 — generosity/endurance. The miser becomes a benefactor; the intolerant becomes patient. The selfish bird that hoarded grain now calls its chicks when it finds corn. The spoiled girl becomes forbearing through hunger, sleeplessness and dishevelment.

chunks.title: Effect 4 — inspiration
chunks.text: Effect 4 — inspiration. Hafiz: the nightingale learnt its song by the favour of the rose. 'Allamah Tabataba'i: Majnun did not go mad by himself — it was the glance of Layla.

chunks.title: Love awakens sleeping powers and frees chained forces, like the splitting of the atom
chunks.text: Love awakens sleeping powers and frees chained forces, like the splitting of the atom. It builds heroes; poets, philosophers and artists have been created by it. At its highest it brings miracles and supernatural events.

chunks.title: Love as cathartic: it purges envy, avarice, cowardice, laziness, conceitedness, self-admiration; removes grudges and malevolence
chunks.text: Love as cathartic: it purges envy, avarice, cowardice, laziness, conceitedness, self-admiration; removes grudges and malevolence. But deprivation/frustration in love may produce complexes and aversions.

chunks.title: Body vs spirit — opposite effects
chunks.text: Body vs spirit — opposite effects. In the spirit: development and thriving. In the body: melting and decomposition — pallor, emaciation, disorder of the digestive and nervous systems; 'perhaps all the effects which it has in the body are destructive'. In the spirit it depends on the object of love and how the person responds to it.

chunks.title: Love removes dassa (Qur'an 91:10) — adulterations of purity with impurity; it destroys deceit and purifies the cheat.
chunks.text: Love removes dassa (Qur'an 91:10) — adulterations of purity with impurity; it destroys deceit and purifies the cheat.

akhlaq.lesson: Use love as a force for purification: choose worthy objects of love and allow that relationship to weaken selfishness, envy, cowardice, and complacency.

units.title: Breaking Down the Barriers

chunks.title: Love brings man out of egoism and self-love — irrespective of the kind of love (animal/sexual, animal/parental, or human) and irrespective o
chunks.text: Love brings man out of egoism and self-love — irrespective of the kind of love (animal/sexual, animal/parental, or human) and irrespective of the beloved's qualities.

chunks.title: Self-love is a limitation and a defensive barrier
chunks.text: Self-love is a limitation and a defensive barrier. Until a man goes outside himself he is timid, avaricious, covetous, misanthropic, quick-tempered, selfish, arrogant; his spirit gives out no spark, has no vivacity, is 'always cold and cut off'. As soon as he steps outside, these qualities are destroyed.

chunks.title: Crucial clarification: self-love in the sense of something to be eliminated does not really exist
chunks.text: Crucial clarification: self-love in the sense of something to be eliminated does not really exist. It makes no sense for a human being to try not to like himself. Amour-propre — esteem for oneself — has not been mistakenly overlooked such that we must throw it out.

chunks.title: The reform of man does not lie in reducing him; it lies in perfecting and adding to him
chunks.text: The reform of man does not lie in reducing him; it lies in perfecting and adding to him. Creation's assignment to man is in the direction of the course of creation — perfection and growth, not decrease and reduction.

chunks.title: Therefore the struggle with self-love is the struggle with the limitations of the self
chunks.text: Therefore the struggle with self-love is the struggle with the limitations of the self. The defensive structure that treats everything not connected to the individual as foreign, 'not me', alien, must be broken down. The personality must expand to take in every other human being, if not the whole universe of creation.

chunks.title: Self-love is thus 'nothing else but a limitation of the conceptual and motivational process'
chunks.text: Self-love is thus 'nothing else but a limitation of the conceptual and motivational process'. Love turns affections and drives outward, enlarges existence and changes the focal point of one's being.

chunks.title: Hence love is a great moral and educative factor — on condition that it is well guided and correctly used (which sets up Ch
chunks.text: Hence love is a great moral and educative factor — on condition that it is well guided and correctly used (which sets up Ch. 10).

akhlaq.lesson: Break the defensive limits of the ego by widening concern beyond the self; love should enlarge responsibility rather than merely satisfy attachment.

units.title: Constructive or Destructive?

chunks.title: Definition: when affection for an individual or thing reaches the summit of intensity, conquers a man's existence and becomes 'the absolute
chunks.text: Definition: when affection for an individual or thing reaches the summit of intensity, conquers a man's existence and becomes 'the absolute ruler over his being', it is called love. Love is the peak of affection.

chunks.title: But love is of TWO completely opposite kinds — the good effects catalogued earlier belong to one kind only; the other has 'completely destru
chunks.text: But love is of TWO completely opposite kinds — the good effects catalogued earlier belong to one kind only; the other has 'completely destructive and opposite effects'.

chunks.title: Kind 1 — the passions
chunks.text: Kind 1 — the passions. Shared with animals, but in man reaches a peak of indescribable intensity, hence also called love. In reality 'a torrent, a bursting forth, a tempest of the passions'. It originates from sexuality and ends there; its rise and fall are largely tied to the physiological activity of the genital organs and to the years of youth; it diminishes with age, and with satiation and separation. A youth quivering at a beautiful face should know 'there is nothing more operating here than a material, animal process'. It comes quickly and goes quickly, cannot be depended on or recommended, has dangers, and kills virtue.

chunks.title: Kind 2 — noble sentiment, Qur'anically muwaddah wa rahmah (30:21)
chunks.text: Kind 2 — noble sentiment, Qur'anically muwaddah wa rahmah (30:21). Here the beloved receives respect and eminence; the lover seeks that person's happiness and is prepared to sacrifice for it. Produces purity, sincerity, tenderness, compassion, altruism — as opposed to the first kind which creates crudeness, savagery and criminality. Examples: a mother's love for her child; devotion to the pure ones and men of God; patriotism; love of principles.

chunks.title: Durability test: the second kind is durable and becomes stronger and warmer with union; the first is impermanent and 'union is reckoned to b
chunks.text: Durability test: the second kind is durable and becomes stronger and warmer with union; the first is impermanent and 'union is reckoned to be its graveyard'.

chunks.title: Qur'anic significance: marriage described as mawaddah wa rahmah is 'a very great point' — it shows the human, higher-than-animal aspect of m
chunks.text: Qur'anic significance: marriage described as mawaddah wa rahmah is 'a very great point' — it shows the human, higher-than-animal aspect of married life; the fundamental link is purity, sincerity and union of two spirits, not the passions, which animals also have.

chunks.title: Rumi: 'Wrath and passion are the attributes of beasts, / Love and compassion the attributes of man.'
chunks.text: Rumi: 'Wrath and passion are the attributes of beasts, / Love and compassion the attributes of man.'

chunks.title: Bertrand Russell (Marriage and Morals): love is worthless when merely possessive — on a level with purely pecuniary work; it must 'feel the
chunks.text: Bertrand Russell (Marriage and Morals): love is worthless when merely possessive — on a level with purely pecuniary work; it must 'feel the ego of the beloved person as important as one's own ego'.

chunks.title: The careful qualification — can passionate love ever help? Yes, but only when linked to piety and modesty, under conditions of separation an
chunks.text: The careful qualification — can passionate love ever help? Yes, but only when linked to piety and modesty, under conditions of separation and inaccessibility, where the spirit bears the pressure without succumbing. Hence the mystics' 'allegorical love turns into real love', and the tradition: he who loves, conceals it, remains chaste, and dies in that state, dies a martyr.

chunks.title: But it must never be RECOMMENDED
chunks.text: But it must never be RECOMMENDED. It is 'a dangerous valley to enter'. Analogy: an affliction may perfect a soul that resists it with patience — but one cannot recommend an affliction, nor manufacture one for oneself or inflict one on another. Russell agrees: suffering energises, but he will not make that a pretext for causing others suffering, since it often destroys instead.

chunks.title: Love vs reason: love 'more than any other factor, is against reason' — wherever it sets foot it ousts reason from its governing position
chunks.text: Love vs reason: love 'more than any other factor, is against reason' — wherever it sets foot it ousts reason from its governing position. Hence love and reason are the famous rivals in mystic literature, and the antagonism of philosophers and mystics originates here. Russell: love 'has a propensity for anarchy'.

chunks.title: Defence of the philosophers: some jurists objected to philosophers who expounded love's benefits in metaphysics — but those philosophers onl
chunks.text: Defence of the philosophers: some jurists objected to philosophers who expounded love's benefits in metaphysics — but those philosophers only noted its useful effects under conditions of piety and chastity, without recommending it, exactly as one would with afflictions. So the objection is invalid.

akhlaq.lesson: Distinguish transformative love from possessive passion: seek the beloved's good rather than using another person or ideal for self-gratification.

units.title: Love and Devotion to Those Close to God

chunks.title: Beyond animal loves (sexual, parental) there is a love 'situated in a more rarefied atmosphere, completely beyond the confines of matter'
chunks.text: Beyond animal loves (sexual, parental) there is a love 'situated in a more rarefied atmosphere, completely beyond the confines of matter'. It originates from an instinct far above the preservation of generations and is what separates the universe of man from the universe of animals: falling in love with excellence, goodness, virtue, and the beauty of reality.

chunks.title: Rumi's test of a worthy object: loves that are 'for the sake of a colour' are not love and end in disgrace; love of the dead is not enduring
chunks.text: Rumi's test of a worthy object: loves that are 'for the sake of a colour' are not love and end in disgrace; love of the dead is not enduring because the dead never come back. Choose the love of that Living One Who is everlasting.

chunks.title: The Qur'anic verses on mahabbah fall into three groups:
chunks.text: The Qur'anic verses on mahabbah fall into three groups:

chunks.title: (1) Believers' love for God/each other: 'those that believe love Allah more ardently' (2:165); the Ansar who love the emigrants and prefer o
chunks.text: (1) Believers' love for God/each other: 'those that believe love Allah more ardently' (2:165); the Ansar who love the emigrants and prefer others above themselves though poverty be their portion (59:9).

chunks.title: (2) God's love for believers: He loves those who repent and cleanse themselves (2:222); the good-doers (3:148, 5:13); those who guard themse
chunks.text: (2) God's love for believers: He loves those who repent and cleanse themselves (2:222); the good-doers (3:148, 5:13); those who guard themselves (9:4,7); those who cleanse themselves (9:108); the just (49:9, 60:8).

chunks.title: (3) Reciprocal/two-way love: 'Say: if you love Allah, follow me, and Allah will love you' (3:31); 'Allah will bring a people He loves, and w
chunks.text: (3) Reciprocal/two-way love: 'Say: if you love Allah, follow me, and Allah will love you' (3:31); 'Allah will bring a people He loves, and who love Him' (5:54); 'unto them the All-merciful shall assign love' (19:96); 'He has set between you love and compassion' (30:21).

chunks.title: Love is what Ibrahim sought for his offspring (14:37) and what the last Prophet was ordered to seek for his kinsmen (42:23).
chunks.text: Love is what Ibrahim sought for his offspring (14:37) and what the last Prophet was ordered to seek for his kinsmen (42:23).

chunks.title: The Khurasani traveller: a man walked from Khurasan on foot to Imam al-Baqir; his feet were cut, showing through his shoes
chunks.text: The Khurasani traveller: a man walked from Khurasan on foot to Imam al-Baqir; his feet were cut, showing through his shoes. 'By God, the only thing that brought me is love of you, the Household.' The Imam: 'By God, if a stone loved us, God would unite it with us. Is the religion other than love?'

chunks.title: The naming question: a man told Imam al-Sadiq, 'We have named our children after you and your fathers; will this benefit us?' — 'Yes, by God
chunks.text: The naming question: a man told Imam al-Sadiq, 'We have named our children after you and your fathers; will this benefit us?' — 'Yes, by God; is the religion other than love?' — citing 3:31 as evidence.

chunks.title: Love produces obedience: 'the lover does not have the power to refuse the wishes of the one he loves'
chunks.text: Love produces obedience: 'the lover does not have the power to refuse the wishes of the one he loves'. Imam al-Sadiq: 'Disobey God and show that you love Him; by my life, that is something amazing. If your love were true, you would have obeyed Him, for the lover is submissive before the one whom he loves.'

akhlaq.lesson: Let devotion to people close to God lead to Godward imitation and service, not personality worship detached from the qualities being loved.

units.title: The Power of Love in Society

chunks.title: The best societies are administered by the power of love — running both ways: the leader's love for the people and the people's devotion to
chunks.text: The best societies are administered by the power of love — running both ways: the leader's love for the people and the people's devotion to the leader.

chunks.title: Without that factor a leader cannot, or finds it very difficult to, lead society, train law-abiding individuals, or even establish justice a
chunks.text: Without that factor a leader cannot, or finds it very difficult to, lead society, train law-abiding individuals, or even establish justice and equality. With it, people become law-minded because affection attracts them to obedience.

chunks.title: Qur'an 3:159 tells the Prophet he holds a great power for influencing people: 'It is by some mercy of Allah that thou art gentle to them; ha
chunks.text: Qur'an 3:159 tells the Prophet he holds a great power for influencing people: 'It is by some mercy of Allah that thou art gentle to them; hadst thou been harsh and hard of heart, they would have scattered from about thee. So pardon them, and pray forgiveness for them, and take counsel with them in the affair.' Pardon, seeking forgiveness, and consultation are all effects of love — as are tolerance, patience and forbearance.

chunks.title: Qur'an 41:34: 'Not equal are the good deed and the evil deed
chunks.text: Qur'an 41:34: 'Not equal are the good deed and the evil deed. Repel with that which is fairer, and behold, he between whom and thee there is enmity shall be as if he were a loyal friend.'

chunks.title: Rumi: 'By the sword of clemency he redeemed so many throats… The sword of clemency is sharper than the sword of iron; nay, it is more produc
chunks.text: Rumi: 'By the sword of clemency he redeemed so many throats… The sword of clemency is sharper than the sword of iron; nay, it is more productive of victory than a hundred armies.' And: 'Chain the neck of the enemy with mercy, which noose no blade can cut.'

chunks.title: 'Ali's firman to Malik al-Ashtar on the governorship of Egypt (Nahj al-Balaghah, Letter 53): 'Awaken in your heart mercy for your subjects a
chunks.text: 'Ali's firman to Malik al-Ashtar on the governorship of Egypt (Nahj al-Balaghah, Letter 53): 'Awaken in your heart mercy for your subjects and love for them and kindness towards them… give them of your forgiveness and your pardon, just as you would like Allah to give you of His forgiveness and pardon.'

chunks.title: The decisive claim: power and force are not enough
chunks.text: The decisive claim: power and force are not enough. 'People can be driven like sheep by power and force, but their inner strengths cannot be awakened and put to use.' And — strikingly — even justice is not enough if it is lifelessly enforced. The ruler must love the people from his heart like a loving father, show that affection, and have an attractive personality that fosters devotion, so as to make use of their wills, ambitions and great human strengths for his divine aim.

akhlaq.lesson: Lead through affection and mercy without abandoning justice; authority becomes formative when people experience both principled standards and genuine care.

units.title: The Best Means for Refining the Soul

chunks.title: The book's central question, stated here: is love and devotion to those near God an aim in itself, or a means for refining the soul, reformi
chunks.text: The book's central question, stated here: is love and devotion to those near God an aim in itself, or a means for refining the soul, reforming morals, and acquiring virtues? (Answer: a means.)

chunks.title: Animal love fixes on the beloved's form, harmony of limbs, colour of skin; once the instinct is satisfied the fire cools and is extinguished
chunks.text: Animal love fixes on the beloved's form, harmony of limbs, colour of skin; once the instinct is satisfied the fire cools and is extinguished. Human love is 'life and vitality; it engenders obedience and loyalty'.

chunks.title: The mechanism — RESEMBLANCE
chunks.text: The mechanism — RESEMBLANCE. Human love 'makes the lover resemble the loved one', a manifestation and copy of the beloved's behaviour. Khwajah Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (commentary on Ibn Sina's Isharat): the soul's love has its source in 'the essential resemblance of the soul of the lover with the soul of the beloved'; it makes the soul tender, yearning, ecstatic, and detaches it from the world's distractions.

chunks.title: Love is 'like an electric wire which joins the being of the beloved to the lover and transfers the qualities of the beloved to him' — 'and i
chunks.text: Love is 'like an electric wire which joins the being of the beloved to the lover and transfers the qualities of the beloved to him' — 'and it is here that the choice of a beloved is of fundamental importance.'

chunks.title: Hence Islam's heavy emphasis on choosing friends and companions — warnings against befriending rotten people, calls to pure-hearted friendsh
chunks.text: Hence Islam's heavy emphasis on choosing friends and companions — warnings against befriending rotten people, calls to pure-hearted friendship.

chunks.title: Ibn 'Abbas: asked who is the best companion, the Prophet replied: 'That person who when you see him, you are reminded of God; when he speaks
chunks.text: Ibn 'Abbas: asked who is the best companion, the Prophet replied: 'That person who when you see him, you are reminded of God; when he speaks, your knowledge increases; when he acts, you fall to thinking of the hereafter and the Resurrection.'

chunks.title: THE SOCRATIC / INTELLECTUAL METHOD
chunks.text: THE SOCRATIC / INTELLECTUAL METHOD. Reform yourself by intellect and devising: gain faith in purification's benefits, then find blameworthy qualities one by one with the instrument of the intellect and cleanse them — like picking hairs from inside one's nose one by one, a farmer pulling tares by hand, or cleaning wheat of stones and soil by hand. Philosophers reform by argument: continence brings honour, greed brings inferiority, knowledge is 'the seal of the kingdom of Solomon', envy is a spiritual sickness, etc.

chunks.title: Mutahhari's assessment: the way of intellect is a correct way and a good means — but the question is its comparative value
chunks.text: Mutahhari's assessment: the way of intellect is a correct way and a good means — but the question is its comparative value. 'Just as a car is a good means, but when compared to an airplane we must examine carefully the extent of its value.' He adds: 'Perhaps it should be said that it is not possible for the intellect to acquit itself of this task', and notes countless competing ethical schools, still unresolved as argument. Sufi line: 'The leg of the reasoners is of wood; a wooden leg is very infirm.'

chunks.title: THE WAY OF LOVE
chunks.text: THE WAY OF LOVE. Mystics recommend finding a perfect being and hanging 'the halter of love for, and fellowship with, him round one's heart' — both less dangerous and swifter.

chunks.title: The three images: (a) hand-work vs machine; (b) the etcher removing unwanted plate material with strong acid, not a nail or knife-point; (c)
chunks.text: The three images: (a) hand-work vs machine; (b) the etcher removing unwanted plate material with strong acid, not a nail or knife-point; (c) separating iron filings from dust by hand — 'how excruciating and troublesome!' — versus one sweep of a powerful magnet. Love is 'an automatic apparatus which gathers the vices together by itself and ejects them'.

chunks.title: Experience has shown those on this path that companionship with the pure affected their spirits to an extent 'which reading hundreds of volu
chunks.text: Experience has shown those on this path that companionship with the pure affected their spirits to an extent 'which reading hundreds of volumes on ethics has not'.

chunks.title: Involuntary imitation: followers imitate a great person's walking, dressing, meeting people, gesturing — 'not voluntary, it is automatic and
chunks.text: Involuntary imitation: followers imitate a great person's walking, dressing, meeting people, gesturing — 'not voluntary, it is automatic and by the force of nature'.

chunks.title: Rumi and Shams: Rumi was a calm scholar teaching quietly in a corner of his town
chunks.text: Rumi and Shams: Rumi was a calm scholar teaching quietly in a corner of his town. From the day he met Shams-e Tabrizi, 'his manner completely changed and a fire flared up inside him' — 'like a fuse which has fallen into a gunpowder store'. He composed the Divan of Shams in his beloved's memory.

chunks.title: THE BALANCE: 'exertion and being drawn, or action and attraction must go together
chunks.text: THE BALANCE: 'exertion and being drawn, or action and attraction must go together. Nothing can be accomplished from effort without attraction, just as being drawn where there is no effort will not reach its aim.'

chunks.title: LOVE'S DEFECT
chunks.text: LOVE'S DEFECT. Hubb al-shay' yu'mi wa yusimm — 'Love of anything brings a blindness and a deafness.' And: 'Anyone who loves something, his sight becomes defective and his heart sick.' Sa'di: 'one's own mind seems perfect and one's own child beautiful.'

chunks.title: Reconciling this with love sharpening perception: love does sensitise intelligence (bringing man out of slow-wittedness, actualising potenti
chunks.text: Reconciling this with love sharpening perception: love does sensitise intelligence (bringing man out of slow-wittedness, actualising potential) — the defect is not dullness but heedlessness. 'Love makes the understanding more keen, but the attention one-sided and one-tracked' — the defect arises from the very singleness that is love's strength.

chunks.title: Worse: love doesn't only cause defectiveness, it shows defects as good — 'it turns one speck of goodness into the sun… makes black seem whit
chunks.text: Worse: love doesn't only cause defectiveness, it shows defects as good — 'it turns one speck of goodness into the sun… makes black seem white and darkness light.' Vahshi: 'If you sat in the ball of my eye, naught would you see but the goodness of Layla.'

chunks.title: Deep point: unlike knowledge, which is a function of the known, love's inward/psychic aspect is greater than its outward/real aspect — its e
chunks.text: Deep point: unlike knowledge, which is a function of the known, love's inward/psychic aspect is greater than its outward/real aspect — its equilibrium is 'not a function of the scales of goodness, but more a function of the scales of the potentiality and essence of the lover'. The lover has a latent fire seeking an object; on finding compatibility (whose secret is unknown — hence love is 'unreasonable'), his inner potentiality manifests and creates goodness according to its own ability, not according to what exists in the beloved.

akhlaq.lesson: Combine intellectual self-examination with the transformative power of worthy companionship; neither analysis nor affection should become an excuse for passivity.

units.title: Examples from the History of Islam

chunks.title: The framing distinction: pupils of philosophers are just students, and philosophers have no more influence than a teacher
chunks.text: The framing distinction: pupils of philosophers are just students, and philosophers have no more influence than a teacher. The prophets' influence is like that of a beloved who has entered the depths of the lover's spirit, caught him, and taken hold of every element of his life.

chunks.title: ABU DHARR AT TABUK
chunks.text: ABU DHARR AT TABUK. The march to Tabuk (~400 miles north of Medina): no equipment, food so short that some made do with a single date, yet all 'full of vigour and cheerful' — 'love created their strength and the force of attraction of the Prophet gave them their power'. Three men fell behind; each time the Prophet said: 'If there is any good in him, God will make him come back; and if there is no good in him, it is better that he go.' Abu Dharr's thin camel gave out; he freed it, shouldered the pack himself, and walked the scorching sand. Finding rainwater among rocks, he refused to drink until his friend the Prophet had drunk, filled his water-skin and carried that too. Nearly collapsing on arrival, offered water, he said in a feeble voice that he had water with him. The Prophet: 'You have water, but you are near to dying from thirst!'

chunks.title: BILAL AL-HABASHI
chunks.text: BILAL AL-HABASHI. Tortured by the Quraysh on scorching stones under the burning sun to make him name the idols and renounce Muhammad. Abu Bakr counselled him to hide his belief from them — but 'love was ever rebellious and deadly'. Bilal repented of dissimulating repeatedly, then became 'quit of repenting' and cried out: 'O Muhammad!… How should there be room therein for repentance? How should I repent of the life everlasting?' Rumi devotes part of Mathnavi bk. 6 to him.

chunks.title: THE RAID OF AR-RAJI' (3 AH)
chunks.text: THE RAID OF AR-RAJI' (3 AH). Men of the 'Adal and al-Qarah tribes asked the Prophet for teachers of Islam. He sent six companions under Marthad ibn Abi Marthad al-Ghanawi (or 'Asim ibn Thabit). At ar-Raji' the Hudhayl fell on them with drawn swords; the delegation had either intended treachery from the start or changed heart. Three — including 'Asim ibn Thabit — refused 'the shame of a pact with polytheists' and fought to the death. Three surrendered: Zayd ibn ad-Dathinnah, Khubayb ibn 'Adiy, 'Abdullah ibn Tariq. 'Abdullah freed a hand near Mecca and reached for his sword; they stoned him to death. Zayd and Khubayb were traded for two Hudhayl captives.

chunks.title: ZAYD'S ANSWER
chunks.text: ZAYD'S ANSWER. Bought by Safwan ibn Umayyah to avenge his father, taken outside Mecca, walking to execution 'with his courageous gait… not trembling even the slightest'. Abu Sufyan, hoping for remorse: 'don't you wish Muhammad were here in your place so we might cut off his head, and you were with your family?' Zayd: 'By God, I don't wish that Muhammad now were in the place he occupies and that a thorn could hurt him, and that I were sitting with my family.' Abu Sufyan, mouth agape, to the Quraysh: 'By God, I swear I have never seen a man who was loved as Muhammad's companions love him.'

chunks.title: KHUBAYB
chunks.text: KHUBAYB. Asked to pray two rak'ah before execution; prayed 'in all humility, respect and absorption', then said: 'were it not that you would think I only delayed out of fear of death, I would have prolonged my prayer.' Condemned to crucifixion, he prayed: 'O God! We have delivered the message of Thy Messenger; so tell him tomorrow what has been done to us…'

chunks.title: SA'D IBN AR-RABI' AT UHUD
chunks.text: SA'D IBN AR-RABI' AT UHUD. Uhud ended sorrowfully — seventy martyred including Hamzah — after a group abandoned their hill position. Sa'd lay with twelve mortal wounds. Told the rumour that the Prophet had been killed, he said: 'Even if Muhammad has been killed, the God of Muhammad has not; the religion of Muhammad remains too. Why do you not stay and defend your religion?' The Prophet later sent an Ansari to find him; Sa'd sent back his greeting and a message to the Ansar and companions: 'You have no excuse with God if anything has happened to your Prophet while you can flutter an eyelid.'

chunks.title: IBN ABI'L-HADID on the Prophet's attraction: nobody heard him speak without love taking a place in his heart
chunks.text: IBN ABI'L-HADID on the Prophet's attraction: nobody heard him speak without love taking a place in his heart. The Quraysh called the Muslims around Mecca subat — 'the infatuated ones'. They feared that if al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, 'the cream of the Quraysh', gave his heart, all Quraysh would follow. They called his speech 'magic, it inebriates more than wine', forbade their sons to sit with him, stuck their fingers in their ears near the Ka'bah so as not to be 'bewitched', and covered their faces lest his appearance draw them — yet most believed after hearing him once.

chunks.title: Historical significance: the revolution Islam created among pre-Islamic Arabs should, by ordinary reckoning, have required generations — let
chunks.text: Historical significance: the revolution Islam created among pre-Islamic Arabs should, by ordinary reckoning, have required generations — letting the vice-habituated generation die out. That it happened fast is explained by the power of attraction: 'like tongues of fire it burns away the roots of evil'. 'It was by riding on the steed of love that such a long way was covered in such a small time.'

akhlaq.lesson: Learn from historical examples by asking what kind of love produced courage, sacrifice, patience, and faithful action under pressure.

units.title: Love for 'Ali in the Qur'an and Sunnah

chunks.title: The set-up: love for the pure ones has been shown to be a means of reform, not an end
chunks.text: The set-up: love for the pure ones has been shown to be a means of reform, not an end. Now: has Islam designated someone we should love?

chunks.title: The wage verse (42:23): all previous prophets said 'we ask no wage from people; our reward is from God' — but the Seal of the Prophets is to
chunks.text: The wage verse (42:23): all previous prophets said 'we ask no wage from people; our reward is from God' — but the Seal of the Prophets is told: 'Say: I do not ask of you a wage for this, except love for (my) relatives (al-mawaddah fi'l-qurba).' Why did he alone ask a wage?

chunks.title: The Qur'an answers itself (34:47): 'Say: I have asked no wage of you; that shall be yours
chunks.text: The Qur'an answers itself (34:47): 'Say: I have asked no wage of you; that shall be yours. My wage falls only upon God.' I.e. the 'wage' accrues to you, not to me — this friendship is 'a halter for your own perfection and reformation'. It is in fact another good he recommends, since the Household are people 'who do not gather round defilement, and whose hems are clean and pure'. Love for them 'brings no other result apart from obedience to the truth and adherence to virtues, and it is friendship for them which transmutes and perfects like the elixir'.

chunks.title: Whatever 'relatives' means, the most obvious referent is 'Ali.
chunks.text: Whatever 'relatives' means, the most obvious referent is 'Ali.

chunks.title: Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (a Sunni authority) is quoted at length: Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf relates that when the verse came down they asked 'W
chunks.text: Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (a Sunni authority) is quoted at length: Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf relates that when the verse came down they asked 'Who are the relatives whose love is due?' — the Prophet said: ''Ali and Fatimah and their sons.' Razi reasons: (1) the verse itself; (2) the Prophet demonstrably loved Fatimah ('Fatimah is a part of my body; what harms her harms me'), and 'Ali and the Hasanayn, by mutawatir traditions — therefore friendship for them is obligatory on all the community, since the Qur'an commands 'follow him' (7:158) and 'you have a good example in Allah's Messenger' (33:21).

chunks.title: Important footnote: the Prophet's love for them had no personal aspect — not merely because they were his children/grandchildren
chunks.text: Important footnote: the Prophet's love for them had no personal aspect — not merely because they were his children/grandchildren. He loved them because they were exemplary and God loved them; he had other children whom he did not love to this extent and to whom the community owes no such obligation.

chunks.title: Traditions on loving 'Ali: Ibn al-Athir (Usd al-Ghabah): 'O 'Ali, God has embellished you… resignation from the world… On you has been besto
chunks.text: Traditions on loving 'Ali: Ibn al-Athir (Usd al-Ghabah): 'O 'Ali, God has embellished you… resignation from the world… On you has been bestowed the love of the wretched… Content is he who loves you and is a true friend to you; woe betides he who shows enmity towards you and lies about you.' — as-Suyuti: 'Love of 'Ali is faith, and enmity towards him is sedition.' — Abu Na'im (Hilyat al-Awliya'): 'Shall I guide you to something which, if you grasp it after me, you will never go astray? It is 'Ali: love him with the love you have for me, and respect him with the respect you have for me. For God has ordered me through Gabriel to tell you this.'

chunks.title: Scale of the evidence: Mutahhari notes more than ninety traditions on love for Amir al-Mu'minin in authoritative Sunni texts, and al-Majlisi
chunks.text: Scale of the evidence: Mutahhari notes more than ninety traditions on love for Amir al-Mu'minin in authoritative Sunni texts, and al-Majlisi's 123 traditions in Bihar al-Anwar vol. 39.

chunks.title: Looking at 'Ali as worship — from Sunni sources: Muhibb al-Tabari from 'A'ishah — Abu Bakr gazed often at 'Ali's face, saying he heard the P
chunks.text: Looking at 'Ali as worship — from Sunni sources: Muhibb al-Tabari from 'A'ishah — Abu Bakr gazed often at 'Ali's face, saying he heard the Prophet say 'Looking at the face of 'Ali is worship' (~20 further traditions). Ibn Hajar (as-Sawa'iq al-muhriqah) from 'A'ishah: 'The best of my brothers is 'Ali, the best of my paternal uncles is Hamzah, and remembrance of 'Ali and speaking about him is worship.'

chunks.title: The chicken tradition (Anas ibn Malik): Umm Ayman brought a cooked chicken; the Prophet prayed, 'O God! Send the best of Thy slaves that he
chunks.text: The chicken tradition (Anas ibn Malik): Umm Ayman brought a cooked chicken; the Prophet prayed, 'O God! Send the best of Thy slaves that he may share with me in eating this chicken.' 'Ali knocked three times; Anas, hoping for an Ansari, twice turned him away saying the Prophet was busy. The third time the Prophet said: 'Anas, go and open the door and bring him in. You are not the first person to love your own people; that are not one of the Ansar.' (Related in more than eighty narrations in Sunni texts.)

akhlaq.lesson: Keep love for 'Ali tied to the qualities and principles the book presents, so reverence becomes a standard for conduct rather than a verbal affiliation.

units.title: The Secret of 'Ali's Force of Attraction

chunks.title: The question: what is the reason for the love for 'Ali in people's hearts? Nobody has discovered the secret — no one can formulate it as 'if
chunks.text: The question: what is the reason for the love for 'Ali in people's hearts? Nobody has discovered the secret — no one can formulate it as 'if it were like this, that would follow'. But it has one.

chunks.title: Three explanations REJECTED: (a) it is not his body — his body is not among us and we never perceived it with our senses; (b) it is not hero
chunks.text: Three explanations REJECTED: (a) it is not his body — his body is not among us and we never perceived it with our senses; (b) it is not hero-worship, which exists in every nation; (c) it is a mistake to say it is love of moral and human excellence, i.e. a humanistic love.

chunks.title: Why (c) fails — the decisive counterfactual
chunks.text: Why (c) fails — the decisive counterfactual. It is true 'Ali was the manifestation of the perfect man and that men love great human figures. But had he possessed all those excellences — the wisdom and knowledge, self-sacrifice and altruism, humility and modesty, courtesy, kindness and mercy, protection of the weak, justness, liberality and love of freedom, respect for humanity, generosity, bravery, magnanimity and mercy toward enemies, munificence and beneficence — and had not had the divine touch in him, 'it is quite certain that there would not have been the feeling of sympathy and awakening of love that there is today'.

chunks.title: The answer: 'Ali is loved because he had the divine link
chunks.text: The answer: 'Ali is loved because he had the divine link. 'Our hearts are unconsciously completely involved with, and connected to, the Truth, right in their depths, and since they find 'Ali to be a great sign of the Truth and a manifestation of the attributes of the Truth they are in love with him.' The basis is the connection of our souls with the Truth laid in our primordial natures (fitrah) — and since our primordial natures are eternal, love for 'Ali is also eternal.

chunks.title: What gives him a 'resplendent and shining place for ever' is his faith and morality — that is what gives him his divine charisma.
chunks.text: What gives him a 'resplendent and shining place for ever' is his faith and morality — that is what gives him his divine charisma.

chunks.title: Sawdah al-Hamdaniyah extolled 'Ali in front of Mu'awiyah: 'May the blessing of God be vouched to him / Whom the grave took away and with who
chunks.text: Sawdah al-Hamdaniyah extolled 'Ali in front of Mu'awiyah: 'May the blessing of God be vouched to him / Whom the grave took away and with whom justice was interred…'

chunks.title: Sa'sa'ah ibn Suhan al-'Abdi, one of the few present at 'Ali's night burial, put a hand over his heart, threw earth on his head and delivered
chunks.text: Sa'sa'ah ibn Suhan al-'Abdi, one of the few present at 'Ali's night burial, put a hand over his heart, threw earth on his head and delivered a long eulogy: 'You saw what others did not see, and reached what others did not reach… your life was the key to good, the lock against exile; and your death is the key to every evil and the lock against every good. If the people had accepted you, blessings would have showered on them from the heaven and the earth; but they preferred this world to the next.'

chunks.title: Mutahhari's coda: truly they preferred this world, and consequently 'they could not endure the justice and unwaveringness of 'Ali' — 'in the
chunks.text: Mutahhari's coda: truly they preferred this world, and consequently 'they could not endure the justice and unwaveringness of 'Ali' — 'in the end the hand of stiffness and stagnation came out of the sleeve of the people and martyred 'Ali.'

chunks.title: The bridge to Part 2: 'Ali is without equal in having totally selfless friends — and the hands of Ziyad ibn Abih and his son 'Abdullah, Hajj
chunks.text: The bridge to Part 2: 'Ali is without equal in having totally selfless friends — and the hands of Ziyad ibn Abih and his son 'Abdullah, Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, al-Mutawakkil, and at the head of them all Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan are 'stained with the blood of these human lives up to their elbows'.

akhlaq.lesson: Examine the attraction of 'Ali by looking at the qualities that survive time: truth, faith, justice, courage, selflessness, and service rather than mere charisma.

units.title: How 'Ali Made Enemies (Part 2 opens)

chunks.title: Scope: the discussion is restricted to his somewhat more than four-year caliphate — though 'Ali was always two-powered
chunks.text: Scope: the discussion is restricted to his somewhat more than four-year caliphate — though 'Ali was always two-powered. From the beginning of the Islamic age one group gravitated to him and another 'were occasionally pained by his existence'. The caliphate simply gave both powers greater manifestation, since before it his links with society — and so his attraction and repulsion — were fewer.

chunks.title: Making enemies is 'another one of his great glories.' Every principled man with an aim — especially the revolutionary — makes enemies
chunks.text: Making enemies is 'another one of his great glories.' Every principled man with an aim — especially the revolutionary — makes enemies. Qur'anic warrant: they struggle in the way of Allah, not fearing the reproach of any reproacher (5:54).

chunks.title: The sting: 'If 'Ali's personality were not distorted today, but were presented just as it was, many of those who pretend to be his friends w
chunks.text: The sting: 'If 'Ali's personality were not distorted today, but were presented just as it was, many of those who pretend to be his friends would take a stand alongside his enemies.'

chunks.title: THE YEMEN GARMENTS INCIDENT
chunks.text: THE YEMEN GARMENTS INCIDENT. 'Ali commanded an army to Yemen; returning toward Mecca he left a deputy and hurried ahead to report. The deputy distributed the garments among the soldiers so they could enter Mecca in new clothes. 'Ali objected and reproved him: no decision should have been taken before the Prophet's orders — in 'Ali's eyes this was expropriation from the bayt al-mal without the leader's permission. He ordered the garments removed and stored. The soldiers complained to the Prophet of 'Ali's harshness. The Prophet: 'O men, do not grumble about 'Ali. I swear by Allah that he is more intensely in the way of God than that anyone should complain about him.'

chunks.title: 'Ali had no concern for anyone in the way of God — interest in someone was because of God
chunks.text: 'Ali had no concern for anyone in the way of God — interest in someone was because of God. 'Naturally, such an attitude makes enemies, and it causes offence to souls full of greed and craving.'

chunks.title: Uniqueness of both powers: no companion had such devoted friends, and none had 'such bold and dangerous enemies'
chunks.text: Uniqueness of both powers: no companion had such devoted friends, and none had 'such bold and dangerous enemies'. He was a man 'who, even after his death, had his corpse attacked by enemies' — hence his will that his grave be hidden, known only to his sons, until roughly a century later when the Umayyads were overthrown, the Khawarij broken, and vendettas few — and Imam al-Sadiq indicated the sacred soil.

chunks.title: THE THREE GROUPS HE EXPELLED AND FOUGHT:
chunks.text: THE THREE GROUPS HE EXPELLED AND FOUGHT:

chunks.title: Nakithun ('those who break allegiance') — the people of Jamal
chunks.text: Nakithun ('those who break allegiance') — the people of Jamal. Mentality: money-worshipping, covetous, displayers of prejudice. 'Ali's speeches on justice and equality were aimed chiefly at them.

chunks.title: Qasitun ('those who deviate') — the people of Siffin
chunks.text: Qasitun ('those who deviate') — the people of Siffin. Mentality: politics, deception and sedition; they killed to seize the reins of government and topple 'Ali's rule. Some advised compromise — giving them part of what they wanted — but 'Ali refused: 'he was ready to fight injustice, not to give his signature to it.' His war with them was 'a war with sedition and double-dealing'.

chunks.title: Mariqun ('those who miss the truth of the religion') — the people of Nahrawan, the Khawarij
chunks.text: Mariqun ('those who miss the truth of the religion') — the people of Nahrawan, the Khawarij. Spirit: inadmissible fanaticism, sanctimoniousness, dangerous ignorance.

chunks.title: Mark of his completeness: that he faced all three deviations — worldly/money-loving men, professional hypocritical politicians, and ignorant
chunks.text: Mark of his completeness: that he faced all three deviations — worldly/money-loving men, professional hypocritical politicians, and ignorant deviationist men of false piety.

chunks.title: Why the Khawarij are chosen for study: though overthrown and gone, their thinking took root and their spirit has always existed in the shape
chunks.text: Why the Khawarij are chosen for study: though overthrown and gone, their thinking took root and their spirit has always existed in the shape of sanctimonious persons across fourteen centuries — 'a grave hindrance to the advancement of Islam and the Muslims'.

akhlaq.lesson: Accept that principled leadership will sometimes create enemies; the test is whether repulsion comes from justice and truth rather than arrogance or cruelty.

units.title: How the Khawarij Came Into Existence

chunks.title: Etymology: khawarij = 'rebels', from khuruj = revolt/insurrection
chunks.text: Etymology: khawarij = 'rebels', from khuruj = revolt/insurrection. The footnote distinguishes two near senses of kharaja 'ala: standing up to fight, and disobedience/insubordination. Because they based their rebellion on a belief and religious ideology they became a sect and the name stuck to them alone — later rebels without a creed were not called Khawarij. They never formed a government but did create a school of law and a literature.

chunks.title: THE STRATAGEM AT SIFFIN
chunks.text: THE STRATAGEM AT SIFFIN. On the final day the battle was turning in 'Ali's favour; Mu'awiyah, with 'Amr ibn al-'As, 'was only one step away from defeat' and saw no escape 'except by having recourse to the creation of confusion'. He ordered Qur'ans raised on spear-points, to show they were people of prayer and the Book, and that the Book should arbitrate. Note: 'Ali had proposed this before and they had refused — it was now 'a subterfuge to rescue themselves from a sure defeat'.

chunks.title: 'Ali's response: 'Strike at them! They are using the pages and the paper of the Qur'an as a ruse… When opposed to its truth, the paper and b
chunks.text: 'Ali's response: 'Strike at them! They are using the pages and the paper of the Qur'an as a ruse… When opposed to its truth, the paper and binding of the Qur'an is of no value and worthy of no respect; it is I who am the reality and the true manifestation of the Qur'an.'

chunks.title: THE LEGAL ARGUMENT HE USED — human shields
chunks.text: THE LEGAL ARGUMENT HE USED — human shields. In the jihad section of Islamic law: if the enemy puts Muslim prisoners at the front as a shield and advances behind them, and there is no access to the attacking enemy except through killing those Muslims, then killing them becomes permissible for the vital interests of Islam. They too are soldiers of Islam and become martyrs; but blood money must be paid from the treasury to their relatives. 'Ali notes this is also a definite rule of international law. His a fortiori: if live Muslims may be struck through, then 'there can be no objection made to the paper and bindings of books' — respect for pages is because of their meaning, and today the fight is for that meaning.

chunks.title: The refusal
chunks.text: The refusal. 'The ignorant and uninformed drew down a black curtain in front of their minds.' They answered that fighting the Qur'an is itself a sin and they must kill to prevent it. Only an hour was needed for victory: Malik al-Ashtar had gone out to destroy Mu'awiyah's command pavilion. This group threatened to attack 'Ali from behind, then drew their swords and threatened to hack him to pieces unless Malik was recalled. Malik replied that a few more moments would finish the enemy; word was sent that if he wanted to see 'Ali alive he must return. He returned — 'and the enemies were jubilant that their stratagem had proved efficacious'.

chunks.title: THE ARBITRATION
chunks.text: THE ARBITRATION. 'Ali said they should choose their arbitrator and he would name his own. Without the slightest dispute they unanimously chose 'Amr ibn al-'As — the deviser of the stratagem. 'Ali proposed 'Abdullah ibn al-'Abbas (versed in politics) or Malik al-Ashtar. But 'those fools were looking for someone of their own kind' and insisted on Abu Musa al-Ash'ari — 'a man of no perspicacity who was not on good terms with 'Ali'. 'Ali and his friends tried to enlighten them; they refused anyone else; he told them to do as they wished.

chunks.title: THE DOUBLE-CROSS
chunks.text: THE DOUBLE-CROSS. After months, 'Amr proposed that neither 'Ali nor Mu'awiyah be caliph but a third — surely 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, Abu Musa's son-in-law. Agreed: 'You should remove 'Ali, and I will do the same with Mu'awiyah.' At the assembly 'Amr deferred with flattery — 'You are the respected, white-bearded man, a companion of the Prophet. Never would I presume to speak before you!' Abu Musa deposed 'Ali, removing his ring from his finger as the image. 'Amr then rose, confirmed 'Ali's deposition, and moved his ring from his right hand to his left, saying: 'I set up Mu'awiyah in the caliphate, just as I put this ring on my finger.' Uproar: the people attacked Abu Musa and beat him with whips; he fled to Mecca and 'Amr went to Damascus.

chunks.title: THE MISDIAGNOSIS — the birth of the sect
chunks.text: THE MISDIAGNOSIS — the birth of the sect. The Khawarij saw the scandal and realised their mistake, 'but they could not understand where exactly their error lay'. They did not say their error was falling for the stratagem and halting the war; nor that it was choosing Abu Musa. Instead: appointing any human arbitrator in God's religion was itself unbelief, for the judge is only God, not man.

chunks.title: The demand on 'Ali: 'We did not understand… You have become an unbeliever, and so have we
chunks.text: The demand on 'Ali: 'We did not understand… You have become an unbeliever, and so have we. But we repent; you too should repent.' 'Ali: 'In any situation, repentance is good. We are always repenting for our sins.' Not enough — he must confess arbitration was a sin and repent of that. He refused: it was they who brought it about, and he could not declare sinful what Islam made lawful, nor confess a sin he had not committed.

chunks.title: BIDDING TO GOOD — the two conditions
chunks.text: BIDDING TO GOOD — the two conditions. Al-amr bi'l-ma'ruf requires (1) profound, knowledgeable insight into the religion, and (2) profound insight into how to act. The second depends on two jurisprudential conditions: ihtimal al-ta'thir (the possibility of effective action) and 'adam tarattub al-mafsadah 'alayh (absence of any resulting evil). Without profound religious knowledge, hadith teaches the loss exceeds the benefit.

chunks.title: Why this duty is uniquely conditional: for prayer, fasting, hajj, zakat and jihad, one does not ask whether a useful result will follow — be
chunks.text: Why this duty is uniquely conditional: for prayer, fasting, hajj, zakat and jihad, one does not ask whether a useful result will follow — benefit exists in every duty but discerning it is not the people's responsibility. In bidding to good it is their responsibility: one must look to the result, the reaction, and whether the action serves the interests of Islam and the Muslims. All Islamic sects agree on this condition except the Khawarij, who held it absolute and unconditional — 'one must not sit down and think about it'. Hence they 'terrorized the lands knowing that they would be killed and their blood would be wasted, and knowing that no useful result would come out of their uprising'.

akhlaq.lesson: Diagnose movements by their ideas and consequences, not by slogans alone; understand how the Khawarij emerged from a particular misreading of arbitration.

units.title: The Basis of Khawarij Opinions & Their View of the Caliphate

chunks.title: THE FOUR ROOTS OF KHAWARIJISM:
chunks.text: THE FOUR ROOTS OF KHAWARIJISM:

chunks.title: (a) They regarded 'Ali, 'Uthman, Mu'awiyah, the fighters at Jamal, and all who accepted arbitration as infidels — except those who voted for
chunks.text: (a) They regarded 'Ali, 'Uthman, Mu'awiyah, the fighters at Jamal, and all who accepted arbitration as infidels — except those who voted for arbitration and afterwards repented.

chunks.title: (b) They regarded as infidels anyone who did not believe in the heresy of those named in (a)
chunks.text: (b) They regarded as infidels anyone who did not believe in the heresy of those named in (a). (I.e. dissent from their takfir was itself unbelief.)

chunks.title: (c) Faith was not sincere belief alone but 'putting the commands into action and desisting from the prohibitions' — faith 'a compound thing
chunks.text: (c) Faith was not sincere belief alone but 'putting the commands into action and desisting from the prohibitions' — faith 'a compound thing made up of belief and action'. (Hence major sin expels from Islam.)

chunks.title: (d) Unconditional necessity to revolt against an unjust governor; bidding to good and forbidding evil are conditional on nothing and must be
chunks.text: (d) Unconditional necessity to revolt against an unjust governor; bidding to good and forbidding evil are conditional on nothing and must be carried out in all circumstances.

chunks.title: The consequence: 'these people started their existence from the recognition that all men on earth were infidels, whose blood was of no value
chunks.text: The consequence: 'these people started their existence from the recognition that all men on earth were infidels, whose blood was of no value and who were all condemned to the Fire.'

chunks.title: THEIR VIEW OF THE CALIPHATE — 'the only idea of the Khawarij's that could be interpreted favourably by the modern thinkers of today'
chunks.text: THEIR VIEW OF THE CALIPHATE — 'the only idea of the Khawarij's that could be interpreted favourably by the modern thinkers of today'. Quasi-democratic: the caliph must be chosen by free election; the worthiest is whoever has merit in faith and piety; he may be Qurayshi or not, from a distinguished tribe or an insignificant one, Arab or non-Arab. If after election and allegiance he acts against the community's interests he must be removed — and if he refuses, fought until killed.

chunks.title: Triangulation: this opposes the Shi'ah (caliphate is a divine office; the caliph can only be one nominated by God) and equally the Sunni (in
chunks.text: Triangulation: this opposes the Shi'ah (caliphate is a divine office; the caliph can only be one nominated by God) and equally the Sunni (innama'l-a'immatu min quraysh — 'the leaders are from the Quraysh').

chunks.title: Development: apparently this was not their original view
chunks.text: Development: apparently this was not their original view. Their slogan la hukma illa li'llah, and Nahj al-Balaghah (Sermon 40; Ibn Abi'l-Hadid vol.2 p.308), indicate they first believed society needed no leader or government at all — people should put the Book of God into practice on their own. They later abandoned this and swore allegiance to 'Abdullah ibn al-Wahab.

chunks.title: Their historical verdicts: the caliphates of Abu Bakr and 'Umar were rightful — rightfully elected, never deviating from the best interest
chunks.text: Their historical verdicts: the caliphates of Abu Bakr and 'Umar were rightful — rightfully elected, never deviating from the best interest. 'Uthman's election was rightful, but toward the end of his sixth year he changed direction and ignored the Muslims' interest; he should have been deposed, and since he continued in office he was killed as an unbeliever and his killing was a religious duty. 'Ali's election was rightful, but since he accepted arbitration and did not repent, he too was killed as an unbeliever and his killing was a religious duty. So: they denounced 'Uthman's caliphate after its seventh year and 'Ali's after the arbitration. They abhorred all subsequent caliphs and were always at war with them. (Source: al-Shahrastani, al-Milal wa'l-Nihal.)

chunks.title: THE DECLINE
chunks.text: THE DECLINE. They arose 'towards the end of the fourth decade of the first century of the Hijrah as the result of a dangerous piece of misrepresentation', and before one and a half centuries were over, 'as the result of hysterical temerity and recklessness', they were hunted by the caliphs to annihilation — totally non-existent by the beginning of 'Abbasid rule.

chunks.title: Causes of ruin: their 'relentless and spiritless logic', the severity and harshness of their behaviour, the incompatibility of their ways wi
chunks.text: Causes of ruin: their 'relentless and spiritless logic', the severity and harshness of their behaviour, the incompatibility of their ways with real life, and their impetuosity — which even did away with taqiyah in its true and reasonable sense.

chunks.title: But the after-effect remained: their thinking and beliefs affected the other sects
chunks.text: But the after-effect remained: their thinking and beliefs affected the other sects. 'Even today, ”Nahrawanis” are to be found in abundance, and, just as in the age of 'Ali, these are the most dangerous of Islam's internal enemies' — and there will always be Mu'awiyahs and 'Amr ibn al-'As's to use them when the time is opportune, even while counting them as enemies.

akhlaq.lesson: Separate religious conviction from rigid political or sectarian conclusions; examine how beliefs about faith, sin, authority, and revolt interact.

units.title: Just a Motto? — and 'Ali's Sense of Democracy

chunks.title: WHY STUDY A DEAD SECT? Turning this into a discussion of a religious sect is 'pointless and to no effect, for there is no such sect in exist
chunks.text: WHY STUDY A DEAD SECT? Turning this into a discussion of a religious sect is 'pointless and to no effect, for there is no such sect in existence today'. The value is that the sect is dead but its spirit is not — 'the spirit of Khawarijism has been incarnated in the campaigns of many of us'.

chunks.title: THE MOTTO/SPIRIT DISTINCTION
chunks.text: THE MOTTO/SPIRIT DISTINCTION. A sect may die as to its motto but live in spirit — or the reverse: an ideology may live as a motto while being 'completely dead in spirit'. So one may be counted a follower in name but not in spirit, and vice versa.

chunks.title: Applied to Sunni/Shi'ah
chunks.text: Applied to Sunni/Shi'ah. Shi'ah motto: 'Ali is caliph immediately after the Prophet, designated by divine decree. Sunni position: the legislation has no special provision; choosing a leader was handed to the people, at most from the Quraysh.
