On the companions: the Shi'ah criticise many great figures; the Sunni regard everyone called a 'companion' with 'amazingly extravagant deference', holding all were just and upright.

chunks.title: The raison d'être contrast (memorise): Shi'ite Islam works through criticism, research, putting forth objections and exactitude; Sunni Islam
chunks.text: The raison d'être contrast (memorise): Shi'ite Islam works through criticism, research, putting forth objections and exactitude; Sunni Islam works through finding the most convenient solution, justification after the act, and trust in providence.

chunks.title: The challenge: is it enough, to recognise a man as Shi'ah today, that he says ''Ali is the caliph immediately after the Prophet' — no matter
chunks.text: The challenge: is it enough, to recognise a man as Shi'ah today, that he says ''Ali is the caliph immediately after the Prophet' — no matter what spirit or way of thinking he has?

chunks.title: The original schism, re-described
chunks.text: The original schism, re-described. The majority 'only looked at the superficial aspect', were 'not sufficiently sharp-sighted or penetrating', and 'found the most convenient solution': great men and elders took a certain way, and it cannot be said they erred. The minority said they would respect anyone who respected the truth, but where they saw the fundamentals of Islam violated at the hands of the very people who had long served Islam, they would respect them no longer. 'They said they were partisans of the principles of Islam, not partisans of the personalities of Islam.' Shi'ism was born in this spirit.

chunks.title: Salman, Abu Dharr, al-Miqdad, 'Ammar gathered round 'Ali and left the majority because they were 'men of principle, who knew the fundamental
chunks.text: Salman, Abu Dharr, al-Miqdad, 'Ammar gathered round 'Ali and left the majority because they were 'men of principle, who knew the fundamentals — that they both knew the religion and practiced it'. They would not 'give their seeing and understanding into the hands of others, so that when these people made mistakes they themselves would also make mistakes'.

chunks.title: THE DOUBTING COMPANION AT JAMAL
chunks.text: THE DOUBTING COMPANION AT JAMAL. He saw on one side 'Ali and great figures; on the other 'A'ishah — of whom the Qur'an says the Prophet's wives are as mothers — with Talhah (a forerunner, good record, expert fighter, valuable services) and az-Zubayr (an even better record, who had gathered in 'Ali's house on the day of Saqifah). Mutahhari's fairness: 'this man must not be blamed too much in his confusion. Perhaps if we found ourselves in the same situation… the personalities of Talhah and az-Zubayr would also dazzle our eyes.' We judge easily only because history has clarified matters, or because 'we have been inculcated with the idea… right from our infancy'. 'But in those days, neither of these factors existed.'

chunks.title: 'ALI'S ANSWER — of which Taha Husayn ('Ali wa Banuh, p.40) said that after revelation ceased and the call from heaven ended, no words of suc
chunks.text: 'ALI'S ANSWER — of which Taha Husayn ('Ali wa Banuh, p.40) said that after revelation ceased and the call from heaven ended, no words of such greatness were heard: 'It is you who have been cheated; truth has become an error for you. Truth and falsehood are not to be known by the measure of the power and personality of individuals… individuals must not be made the criteria for truth and falsehood. It is truth and falsehood which should be the standards for individuals and their personalities.'

chunks.title: Consequence: 'Ali 'establishes truth itself as the criterion of truth, and the spirit of Shi'ite Islam is none other than this'
chunks.text: Consequence: 'Ali 'establishes truth itself as the criterion of truth, and the spirit of Shi'ite Islam is none other than this'. The sect is born 'from a special perspicacity and a granting of importance to principles, not from individuals and persons'. Hence 'it is natural that the Shi'ah were the first believers and idol-breakers'.

chunks.title: The generational contrast: after the Prophet's death, 'Ali was thirty-three with a group 'less than the number of the fingers on one's hands
chunks.text: The generational contrast: after the Prophet's death, 'Ali was thirty-three with a group 'less than the number of the fingers on one's hands'; opposing him were men of sixty with a large majority. Majority logic: this is the way of the leaders and shaykhs, and they do not make mistakes, so follow it. Minority logic: that which does not err is the truth; the elders must accord themselves with the truth.

chunks.title: The demand on the Shi'ah: 'the true Shi'ah is a copy of 'Ali's conduct; the Shi'ah must also, like 'Ali, have two sides to his character' —
chunks.text: The demand on the Shi'ah: 'the true Shi'ah is a copy of 'Ali's conduct; the Shi'ah must also, like 'Ali, have two sides to his character' — attraction and repulsion, though 'not any attraction or any repulsion' (attraction can be to falsehood, repulsion from virtue).

chunks.title: Balanced note on the Khawarij: not all elements of their thinking fell under 'Ali's repulsion — 'a good many bright distinctions and positiv
chunks.text: Balanced note on the Khawarij: not all elements of their thinking fell under 'Ali's repulsion — 'a good many bright distinctions and positive points are also to be found in their way of thinking', which, absent the dark points, would have been subject to his attraction. But the dark side was strong enough to place them among his enemies.

chunks.title: 'ALI'S DEMOCRACY
chunks.text: 'ALI'S DEMOCRACY. He treated them 'with the utmost degree of liberality and democracy'. He was caliph, they his subjects; every punitive action was in his power. He did not imprison them, did not flog them, did not even cut off their quota from the bayt al-mal, and looked on them as on anyone else. 'Maybe such a degree of freedom is without precedent in the world.'

chunks.title: They disrupted his speeches and sermons in the mosques
chunks.text: They disrupted his speeches and sermons in the mosques. Once a Kharijite called out during an impromptu answer: 'May God kill this man; what a knowledgeable man he is!' Others moved to restrain him; 'Ali ordered them to release him: 'It was only me he insulted.'

chunks.title: IBN AL-KAWWA' IN THE PRAYER
chunks.text: IBN AL-KAWWA' IN THE PRAYER. They would not pray behind 'Ali, considering him a disbeliever, but came to the mosque to molest him. As 'Ali stood in prayer with the people behind him, Ibn al-Kawwa' shouted Qur'an 39:65 — 'if thou associatest, thy work shall surely fail and thou wilt be among the losers' — insinuating that 'Ali's past services (the brotherhood, laylat al-mabit when he slept in the Prophet's bed as a lure for swords) had been cancelled by his unbelief. 'Ali fell silent each time, obeying 7:204 ('when the Qur'an is recited, give ear to it and be silent'). After several repetitions he recited 30:60 — 'So be thou patient: surely Allah's promise is true; and let not those who have not sure faith make thee unsteady' — then paid no more attention and continued his prayer.

chunks.title: WHAT CHANGED
chunks.text: WHAT CHANGED. 'In the beginning the Khawarij were peaceable, and contented themselves with merely criticizing and speaking openly.' As they despaired of 'Ali repenting, they resolved on revolution. They gathered at a comrade's house for an inflammatory speech: the world must not be dearer to a believer than bidding to good and forbidding evil and speaking truth, 'even though these may bring loss and involve danger'; let us leave this city where injustice dwells for the mountains or other towns and stop these misguided innovations. They then threatened the security of the highways, took to marauding and sedition, aiming to weaken and bring down the government.

chunks.title: 'Now it was no longer the time to leave them at liberty, for it was not a matter of the expression of beliefs, but of sabotage against publi
chunks.text: 'Now it was no longer the time to leave them at liberty, for it was not a matter of the expression of beliefs, but of sabotage against public security and an armed uprising against the legal government.'

chunks.title: NAHRAWAN
chunks.text: NAHRAWAN. 'Ali met them on the banks of the Nahrawan, made a speech of advice and 'an incontrovertible proof', then put the flag of true faith into the hands of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari as a sign that everyone gathering round it was a true believer. Out of twelve thousand, eight thousand turned back; the remainder were obstinate, were severely beaten, and 'apart from a very small band none remained'.

akhlaq.lesson: Preserve both freedom of expression and principled boundaries: disagreement need not become persecution, while armed disorder cannot be treated as mere speech.

units.title: The Distinguishing Features of the Khawarij

chunks.title: Their spirit was 'a mixture of the ugly and the beautiful' — Mutahhari deliberately gives both sides
chunks.text: Their spirit was 'a mixture of the ugly and the beautiful' — Mutahhari deliberately gives both sides. In the end the combination made them 'dangerous and even horrifying', and 'Ali's personality repulsed rather than attracted them.

chunks.title: FEATURE 1 — Struggle and self-sacrifice (positive)
chunks.text: FEATURE 1 — Struggle and self-sacrifice (positive). They strove valiantly for their beliefs; their history contains 'completely altruistic men who have few equals in the history of mankind'. Ibn 'Abdu Rabbih: 'among all the sects, none were more convinced or exerted more effort… none more ready to die'. One, speared deep, rushed toward his killer saying 'O God! I am hurrying towards you so that you may be pleased.' Mu'awiyah sent a father to recall his Kharijite son; the father finally offered to bring the man's infant child to move his fatherly instincts — the son: 'I swear by God, I am more eager for sword-thrusts than for my son!'

chunks.title: FEATURE 2 — Worship and devotion (positive)
chunks.text: FEATURE 2 — Worship and devotion (positive). They spent nights in prayer, with no desire for the world. Ibn 'Abbas's report from Nahrawan: twelve thousand men whose foreheads were calloused by excess of prostration, whose hands had become hard like camels' feet from pressing the burning ground, whose shirts were tattered and worn down to their skins — 'but who were unwavering and determined'. They were strictly obedient to Islam's outward practices and never touched what they considered a sin. Ziyad ibn Abih killed one and asked his slave what kind of man he was: the slave said he had never brought him food by day nor laid his bedding at night — he fasted the days and prayed the nights.

chunks.title: 'ALI'S JUDGEMENT ON THEM: 'Do not kill any Khawarij after me, because one who seeks the truth and errs is not the same as one who seeks fals
chunks.text: 'ALI'S JUDGEMENT ON THEM: 'Do not kill any Khawarij after me, because one who seeks the truth and errs is not the same as one who seeks falsehood and finds it' (Sermon 60). They differed from Mu'awiyah's party: the Khawarij wanted truth but had fallen into error, whereas Mu'awiyah's men 'were imposters from the start whose way was that of falsehood'. Killing Khawarij after 'Ali would therefore benefit Mu'awiyah, who was worse and more dangerous.

chunks.title: THE RAREST THING 'ALI DID
chunks.text: THE RAREST THING 'ALI DID. Against people 'who clung to, and adorned themselves with, the externals of devotion, and whose faces affected truth, whose clothes were in tatters and who were professional worshippers, 'Ali drew his sword'. Mutahhari's honesty: 'if we had been in the place of his companions and had seen the face of these people, our feelings would have been moved, and we would have remonstrated with 'Ali about drawing swords against such people.'

chunks.title: 'Ali's own claim: 'I have put out the eye of revolt (fitnah)
chunks.text: 'Ali's own claim: 'I have put out the eye of revolt (fitnah). No one had the daring to do this except me, when its gloom had surged up and its rabidity had become severe' (Sermon 92). Two images: ghayhab (gloom) — their external saintliness created 'a dark and vague atmosphere… filled with doubt and hesitation' in which even strong believers became uncertain; and kalab (rabidity) — like hydrophobia in a dog that bites all it meets and transmits the disease, so that the bitten become rabid and bite others. Wise men kill a rabid dog at once to save others. 'They were not curable; they bit and infected and regularly added to the number of cases of rabies.'

chunks.title: Why only he could do it: 'Neither their calloused foreheads, nor the ascetic-like clothes, nor their forever God-remembering tongues, nor ev
chunks.text: Why only he could do it: 'Neither their calloused foreheads, nor the ascetic-like clothes, nor their forever God-remembering tongues, nor even their strong and steadfast beliefs, could become an obstacle to my insight.' Apart from 'Ali no believer dared unsheathe a sword against them — 'only someone who did not believe in God and Islam could have dared', i.e. for the wrong reasons. His action then 'smoothed the path' for later caliphs and rulers to fight them, and for others to fight any group outwardly pious but 'really fools'.

chunks.title: Prophetic warrant: 'Two groups will break my back — those who know but act recklessly, and those who are ignorant but profess piety.'
chunks.text: Prophetic warrant: 'Two groups will break my back — those who know but act recklessly, and those who are ignorant but profess piety.'

chunks.title: FEATURE 3 — Ignorance (negative)
chunks.text: FEATURE 3 — Ignorance (negative). They could not understand realities and wrongly interpreted events; this warped understanding hardened into a religion for which they made the greatest sacrifices. Historical explanation: in the whole thirteen-year Meccan period the Prophet permitted no jihad, not even defensive; permission came only in the second year in Medina. That interval let Islam's teachings and spirit 'penetrate into the depths of their spirits', so each companion became a true emissary who knew what he was fighting for. 'Ali: 'They linked their profound understanding with their swords.' But in the time of the caliphs, most attention went to conquests, neglecting the duty to teach Islamic culture and spirit to those newly attracted. The Khawarij — mostly Arabs, some not — were all ignorant of Islam's principles and unacquainted with its culture, and 'wanted to redress all their shortcomings by emphasis on prostration'.

chunks.title: 'Ali on their morale: 'People who are crude, lacking lofty ideas or subtle feelings; people who are feeble, like slaves, rogues assembled fr
chunks.text: 'Ali on their morale: 'People who are crude, lacking lofty ideas or subtle feelings; people who are feeble, like slaves, rogues assembled from every corner… They are people who should first of all be instructed… A guardian should rule over them and take them by the hand; they should not be left free, to keep swords in their hands, and to voice their opinions about Islam. They are neither émigrés nor Ansar.'

chunks.title: The worse offspring: from this pietistic trend came another group without the Khawarij's bravery and self-sacrifice
chunks.text: The worse offspring: from this pietistic trend came another group without the Khawarij's bravery and self-sacrifice. They 'pulled Islam towards monasticism and retreat from the world' and spread pretension and sanctimoniousness. Lacking the courage to wield steel against the powerful, they wielded the sword of words against the learned, making it a custom to call scholars unbelievers, immoralists and irreligious.

chunks.title: The core danger: ignorant pietists 'become tools and instruments in the hands of the cunning, and a barrier to the way which is in the highe
chunks.text: The core danger: ignorant pietists 'become tools and instruments in the hands of the cunning, and a barrier to the way which is in the higher interests of Islam'. 'Ali: 'you are arrows in the hand of Satan which he uses to strike his target, and through you he casts people into confusion and doubt.' And: 'For 'Ali… worship hand in hand with ignorance was of absolutely no value' — he could not separate their devotion from their ignorance because their devotion was the very same as their ignorance, so 'he destroyed them, and they could not use their asceticism, piety and devotion as a shield between themselves and 'Ali'.

chunks.title: THE HUKM ERROR
chunks.text: THE HUKM ERROR. Qur'an 6:57: in al-hukmu illa li'llah — 'The judgement is Allah's alone.' Here hukm means the law and order of man's life, i.e. the right to lay down law, denied to any other than God (or one authorised by Him). The Khawarij took hukm as hukumah (government), also implying hakamiyah (arbitration) — concluding that government, arbitration and leadership, like law-giving, belong to God alone, and no one may arbitrate among or govern people.

chunks.title: 'ALI'S REPLY: 'The sentence is right but what they think it means is wrong.' Law-giving is God's alone, but they say governance is
chunks.text: 'ALI'S REPLY: 'The sentence is right but what they think it means is wrong.' Law-giving is God's alone, but they say governance is. 'The fact is that men need a governor, a ruler, whether he is good or (maybe) bad. Under the shadow of his rule, the believer performs good actions while the disbeliever profits from his worldly life… Through the ruler, taxes are collected, enemies are fought, the roads are kept safe, and the rights of the weak are taken from the strong, so that the virtuous enjoy peace and are given protection from the wicked.' In short: the law does not get put into practice all by itself.

chunks.title: FEATURE 4 — Narrow-mindedness (negative)
chunks.text: FEATURE 4 — Narrow-mindedness (negative). 'Their thought evolved below very inferior horizons'; they 'enclosed Islam and the Muslims within the four walls of their own limited ideas' and claimed everyone else had misunderstood and was destined for Hell. The first thing such a person does is give his narrow-mindedness the form of a religious belief — restricting God's mercy, making Him 'sit forever on a throne of wrath, waiting for his slave to make some error'. Doctrine: the perpetrator of any great sin — lying, backbiting, drinking alcohol — is a kafir, outside Islam, eternally condemned.

chunks.title: 'Ali's two-part refutation (Sermon 126): (1) The Prophet's practice — he punished someone and then read the burial prayers over his corpse,
chunks.text: 'Ali's two-part refutation (Sermon 126): (1) The Prophet's practice — he punished someone and then read the burial prayers over his corpse, which would be forbidden (9:84) if great sin made one an infidel; he lashed the drinker, cut the thief's hand, whipped the adulterer, then gave them all a place in Muslim meetings, did not cut their wages from the bayt al-mal, and married them to other Muslims — meting out punishments without crossing names off the list of the Muslims. (2) The generalisation error — suppose 'Ali had erred and thereby become an infidel: why condemn the whole community? Why carry swords and subject the sinless and the sinners alike to their edge? So he objected on two counts: generalising sin to the guiltless, and equating sin with unbelief.

chunks.title: 'Ali's fight was with a way of thinking, not with individuals — 'if these individuals had not thought in this way, 'Ali would not have behav
chunks.text: 'Ali's fight was with a way of thinking, not with individuals — 'if these individuals had not thought in this way, 'Ali would not have behaved with them in the way he did and split their blood so that these ideas would die with them'.

chunks.title: The takfir tradition continues: 'When 'Ali was charged with being an infidel, the position of others is clear.' Those accused down the centu
chunks.text: The takfir tradition continues: 'When 'Ali was charged with being an infidel, the position of others is clear.' Those accused down the centuries include Ibn Sina, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, Mulla Sadra, Fayd al-Kashani, Sayyid Jamal al-Din al-Asadabadi (al-Afghani), and Muhammad Iqbal. Ibn Sina's verse: 'Calling me an infidel is no easy exaggeration, / For there is no faith stronger than mine. / If at one time there is only one like me and he an infidel, / Was there ever a Muslim in any period?' Tusi, called infidel by one titled Nizam al-'Ulama' ('orderer of the learned'): 'If the “Organiser” who lacks order call me an infidel… I shall call him a Muslim, for there is no answer to a lie except a lie.'

chunks.title: FEATURE 5 — Inflexibility and the sacralising of forms
chunks.text: FEATURE 5 — Inflexibility and the sacralising of forms. They 'started an inflexibility and stagnation completely opposed to the Qur'an's way', conceiving Islamic education as 'deadening and motionless' and dragging 'solid forms and shapes into Islam'. Against this: Islam is never concerned with mere forms; its teachings are directed to spirit and meaning. 'No material means or outward form can occur in Islam with a “sacred” side' — which is precisely why Islam avoids collision with scientific and cultural development and conforms easily to the requirements of the times. Islam gives universals, which can take many outward manifestations without the truth changing; but harmonising truth with its outward referents 'is not such an easy matter that anyone can do it, for it needs penetrating perception and genuine understanding'.

chunks.title: 'ALI'S INSTRUCTION TO IBN 'ABBAS: 'Do not reason with them by the Qur'an, because the Qur'an has many sides to it: you will speak and they w
chunks.text: 'ALI'S INSTRUCTION TO IBN 'ABBAS: 'Do not reason with them by the Qur'an, because the Qur'an has many sides to it: you will speak and they will speak. But reason with them by the sunnah, because they cannot find any escape from that' (Letter 78). Because the Qur'an concerns universals, each side can pick a different referent and argue from it, giving no result; the sunnah is particular and has pointed out the applications.

chunks.title: THE THREE STAGES OF ARBITRATION — the distinction they could not make: (i) 'Ali was not happy to have arbitration and knew the proposal was
chunks.text: THE THREE STAGES OF ARBITRATION — the distinction they could not make: (i) 'Ali was not happy to have arbitration and knew the proposal was a trick and deception, insisting strongly and refusing to be moved. (ii) Once it was decided, he said Abu Musa was incompetent and recommended Ibn 'Abbas or Malik al-Ashtar. (iii) The basis of arbitration is correct and not dangerous — on this he also insisted. Their failure: they 'imagined that since the arbitration had gone wrong in this instance, its whole foundation must have been null and void' — unable to 'differentiate between the universal and its application'.

chunks.title: al-Mubarrad's report (al-Kamil): 'Ali asked them — 'By God, were any of you, like me, against arbitration?' 'By God, you are witness that no
chunks.text: al-Mubarrad's report (al-Kamil): 'Ali asked them — 'By God, were any of you, like me, against arbitration?' 'By God, you are witness that none of us were!' 'Did you not encourage me to accept?' 'By God, you are witness that we did!' 'So why are you against me now?' They answered that they had sinned and repented, and he must too. 'Ali said astaghfiru'llah min kulli dhanbin — and about six thousand returned, ready to march on Damascus. Then al-Ash'ath ibn Qays al-Kindi told 'Ali the people were saying he recognised arbitration as an error and unbelief. 'Ali went up on the minbar: 'Anyone who imagines that I have gone back on the arbitration imagines mistakenly, and anyone who thinks that arbitration is an error is himself in greater error.' The Khawarij left the mosque and rebelled again.

chunks.title: Qur'an vs men as arbitrators
chunks.text: Qur'an vs men as arbitrators. 'Ali: 'We did not name people as arbitrators, but we named the Qur'an as arbitrator. The Qur'an is a book, bound between two covers, and it does not speak. It therefore needs an interpreter. Only men can be such interpreters.' Refusing would have made them the party turning from the Book, since 4:59 commands referring disputes to Allah and the Prophet — Allah meaning decision by the Qur'an, the Prophet meaning his sunnah. 'Now, if arbitration were truly implemented through the Qur'an, we should be the most rightful of people to receive it; and if through the sunnah, we should be the first of them to receive it.'

chunks.title: The Shi'ah objection answered: if rulership and Imamate are by divine designation (nass), how could 'Ali submit to arbitration and then defe
chunks.text: The Shi'ah objection answered: if rulership and Imamate are by divine designation (nass), how could 'Ali submit to arbitration and then defend it? Answer, from his own words: correctly conducted, arbitration by Qur'an or by sunnah could yield no conclusion other than his own right to the caliphate.

akhlaq.lesson: Combine worship with knowledge, courage, humility, and discernment; outward piety without understanding can become dangerous rather than spiritually elevating.

units.title: The Influence of Islamic Sects on Each Other

chunks.title: The core observation: however much sects differ in slogans and principles, 'the spirit of one sect will penetrate into another one, and the
chunks.text: The core observation: however much sects differ in slogans and principles, 'the spirit of one sect will penetrate into another one, and the latter, although it may be an opponent of the first, will absorb its spirit and soul'.

chunks.title: 'The nature of man is a thief' — hence one finds people who are Sunni in name but Shi'ah in spirit, and the reverse; someone dogmatic, legal
chunks.text: 'The nature of man is a thief' — hence one finds people who are Sunni in name but Shi'ah in spirit, and the reverse; someone dogmatic, legalistic and outward in profession but spiritually a Sufi, and vice versa; and — the crucial case — people who are 'Shi'ah by imitation and by their speech, but spiritually and practically Kharijite'. True of individuals, communities and nations alike.

chunks.title: Transmission mechanism: when social groups associate, beliefs spread from one to another even while each tries to preserve its own
chunks.text: Transmission mechanism: when social groups associate, beliefs spread from one to another even while each tries to preserve its own. Mutahhari's controversial example: qama-zani (striking the head with a sword during Muharram mourning) and the beating of drums and blowing of horns penetrated Iran from the Orthodox Christians of Caucasia, and 'since the spirit of the people was receptive to these customs, they spread like wild-fire'.

chunks.title: Therefore: 'the spirit of each sect must be uncovered.' Typology of sect-origins: some are born from a willingness to see the good in certai
chunks.text: Therefore: 'the spirit of each sect must be uncovered.' Typology of sect-origins: some are born from a willingness to see the good in certain events or persons — 'to look upon your brother's deed in the best light' — e.g. the Sunni, 'born of a favorable predisposition towards certain personalities'. Some from emphasis on principles rather than persons, and are critical — like the early Shi'ah. Some from emphasis on inward spirit and its interpretation — the Sufis. Some from emphasis on bigotry and inflexibility — the Khawarij.

chunks.title: Linguistic analogy: ideas pass between sects as words pass between languages without anyone intending it — Arabic words entered Persian afte
chunks.text: Linguistic analogy: ideas pass between sects as words pass between languages without anyone intending it — Arabic words entered Persian after the conquest, and some thousand Persian words entered Arabic; Turkish influenced both (al-Mutawakkil's era, the Seljuqs, the Mongols). The same holds for fashions and tastes.

chunks.title: THE KHARIJITE INHERITANCE — the defining trait: 'the inflexibility of their minds and the disengagement of intellection and religiosity in t
chunks.text: THE KHARIJITE INHERITANCE — the defining trait: 'the inflexibility of their minds and the disengagement of intellection and religiosity in their thought' has leaked into the Islamic community in various forms throughout history. However much other sects considered themselves opponents, 'we can still see the spirit of Kharijism in their ways of thinking'.

chunks.title: A recurring symptom: some 'have always believed that their slogans should battle with anything new', even giving 'a holy aura to the means o
chunks.text: A recurring symptom: some 'have always believed that their slogans should battle with anything new', even giving 'a holy aura to the means of life' and treating the use of every new means as disbelief and atheism — though Islam sanctifies no material means or external form.

chunks.title: THE MU'TAZILAH
chunks.text: THE MU'TAZILAH. Arose at the beginning of the second century AH, in the wake of the debate over whether committing great sins makes one a disbeliever — 'naturally their coming into existence was connected with the Kharijites'. They wanted 'a degree of free thinking' and 'to create an intellectual life'; though lacking a scientific basis, they investigated Islamic problems fairly freely, critically evaluated ahadith, and followed only researched conclusions. They stood against those who based everything on ahadith and against the exoterists, who recognised only the outward meaning, had nothing to do with the spirit or inner meaning of Qur'an and hadith, and denied that clear judgements follow from the intellect.

chunks.title: THE ASH'ARITES
chunks.text: THE ASH'ARITES. After about one and a half centuries of the Mu'tazili school's ups and downs, the Ash'arites arose and 'once again the value of sheer intellectual thinking and reflexion and the reckonings of pure metaphysics were denied'. They held that Muslims must believe the exoteric meanings of traditional explanations and not think or reflect upon deeper meanings; 'every kind of question and answer, or why and wherefore, was an innovation for them'. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, one of the four Sunni Imams, opposed Mu'tazili thinking so strongly that he went to prison and was tortured for it, yet maintained his opposition.

chunks.title: The outcome Mutahhari laments: 'In the end, the Ash'arites were the winners, and the school of intellectual thinking closed down; and this v
chunks.text: The outcome Mutahhari laments: 'In the end, the Ash'arites were the winners, and the school of intellectual thinking closed down; and this victory dealt a great blow to the intellectual life of Islamic sciences.' An Ash'arite poet celebrated: 'The reign of the people of innovation has come to an end… Did they have a jurist / Or an Imam to lead them in their innovations?'

chunks.title: THE AKHBARI SCHOOL
chunks.text: THE AKHBARI SCHOOL. 'Also a kind of dissociation of intellection and religion' — a Shi'ah school of jurists, at its height in the eleventh and twelfth centuries AH (18th CE). They had much in common with the Sunni exoterics and traditionists, following the same method of deriving laws and differing only in which ahadith they chose. They 'completely shut down the work of the intellect', denied any probative value to intellectual perception in deriving rulings, considered following the intellect absolutely forbidden, and campaigned against the Usulis. They held the only proofs were Qur'an and sunnah — but since the Qur'an's probative force came only through hadith exegesis, they 'virtually disregarded the Qur'an as a source of proof and only recognized the outward meaning of ahadith to be trustworthy'.

chunks.title: The point of the survey: not to map Islamic thought exhaustively, but to show 'what the influences of the sects have been on each other, and
chunks.text: The point of the survey: not to map Islamic thought exhaustively, but to show 'what the influences of the sects have been on each other, and that the Kharijite sect, although it did not last long, continued to manifest its spirit in every century and age of Islam up to the present' — where 'a number of contemporary writers and “intellectuals” of the Islamic world have produced their way of thinking in a modern and up-to-date form by associating it with empirical philosophy.'

akhlaq.lesson: Guard against inheriting an enemy's method while opposing the enemy: rigidity and intellectual stagnation can survive inside movements that reject Khawarij labels.

units.title: The Politics of 'Using' the Qur'an & Fighting Hypocrisy

chunks.title: The technique has lasted thirteen centuries
chunks.text: The technique has lasted thirteen centuries. 'Holding the Qur'an upon a spear' becomes 'especially rife among those who wish to profit from it whenever sanctimoniousness and exotericism increases and it becomes fashionable to display one's piety and asceticism.'

chunks.title: LESSON ONE — the ignorant as a ready-made instrument
chunks.text: LESSON ONE — the ignorant as a ready-made instrument. Whenever the ignorant and uninformed 'put on a show of sanctity and piety, and people take them to be the symbol of the practicing Muslim, an excellent tool is available for unscrupulous schemers'. Such schemers 'always turn these people into an instrument for their own ends, and make their presence a strong hindrance to the ideas of real reformers'. It is common to see anti-Islamic elements openly 'setting the power of Islam itself to work against Islam'.

chunks.title: Colonialism: Western colonialism 'has had much experience in the use of this means', profiting from 'deceitful arousal of the sentiments of
chunks.text: Colonialism: Western colonialism 'has had much experience in the use of this means', profiting from 'deceitful arousal of the sentiments of the Muslims, especially in the field of the creation of schisms between them'. The disgrace: Muslims plan to drive out foreign influence and find 'the very people they wanted to save turn into a barrier in their path in the name, and under the banner, of religion'. 'Indeed, if the masses of the people are ignorant and uninformed, hypocrites will use the fortress of Islam itself.' (He then applies this to a contemporary Iranian political controversy.)

chunks.title: The Prophet's warning: 'I am not anxious about the incursion of poverty among my community; that about which I am afraid for them is crooked
chunks.text: The Prophet's warning: 'I am not anxious about the incursion of poverty among my community; that about which I am afraid for them is crooked thinking. That which poverty of thought will bring my community is much worse than that which economic poverty will bring them.'

chunks.title: LESSON TWO — correct methodology of derivation
chunks.text: LESSON TWO — correct methodology of derivation. 'The Qur'an is a leader and a guide when it is subjected to true reflection, when it is interpreted wisely, when guidance is taken from the people who really know the Qur'an, who are firmly rooted in its sciences. As long as our methodology is wrong… we shall not derive any profit from it.' Profiteers or the ignorant read it and 'follow up an incorrect possibility' — Nahj al-Balaghah: 'they say the word “truth”, and then set their minds on falsehood!' 'This is not practicing the Qur'an or bringing it to life, this is putting it to death.'

chunks.title: Why the Qur'an gives universals, not names
chunks.text: Why the Qur'an gives universals, not names. It 'always presents its project in a general and fundamental form', and deducing the particular from the universal 'depends on our correct understanding'. It does not say that in a war on a certain day 'Ali was right; it says (49:9): If two parties of believers fight, put things right between them; then, if one of them is insolent against the other, fight the insolent one till it reverts to Allah's commandment. It 'does not spell out names', nor say that after forty years a man called Mu'awiyah will fight 'Ali and you should side with 'Ali. 'The Qur'an's task is not to make a list of subjects and point out which is right and which is wrong; such a thing would be impossible.' It came to stay forever, so it must make fundamentals clear 'so that falsehood can take its place face to face with truth in every age'.

chunks.title: The duty this imposes: people must open their eyes to the universal and distinguish the terrorizing party from the terrorized; accept it if
chunks.text: The duty this imposes: people must open their eyes to the universal and distinguish the terrorizing party from the terrorized; accept it if the unruly party ceases; but if they 'stop, and try to be cunning so as to save themselves from defeat, and prepare themselves for a new attack', then be firm and do not give way to their cunning. 'It is up to the people themselves to discriminate in all these matters.' The Qur'an seeks that Muslims be intellectually and socially mature, and a necessary consequence of such maturity is the ability to differentiate between the just man and the unjust man. 'The Qur'an did not come to be always for people like a guardian over a juvenile.'

chunks.title: 'Ali (Sermon 146): 'You will never know truth and follow the right way unless you know the person who has abandoned it.' Knowing principles
chunks.text: 'Ali (Sermon 146): 'You will never know truth and follow the right way unless you know the person who has abandoned it.' Knowing principles and generalities is not enough without finding their reference in particulars — 'for it is possible that, through an error of judgement concerning persons and individuals or through ignorance of the situation, one will act in the name of truth and Islam and under the banner of Islam against Islam and truth and for falsehood.'

chunks.title: THE NECESSITY OF FIGHTING HYPOCRISY
chunks.text: THE NECESSITY OF FIGHTING HYPOCRISY. 'The most difficult struggle is the one against hypocrisy, for it is the struggle against the cunning who use the stupid as their weapon.' It is 'several degrees more difficult than the fight with unbelief', because unbelief is 'an unconcealed, open and unhidden current', while the struggle against hypocrisy is a struggle against concealed unbelief.

chunks.title: Hypocrisy has two faces: outward — Islam and Muslim; inward — unbelief and evil
chunks.text: Hypocrisy has two faces: outward — Islam and Muslim; inward — unbelief and evil. Spotting the latter is very difficult for ordinary people and sometimes impossible, so 'the struggle with hypocrisy ends in failure because the great majority of people cannot extend the reach of their perception beyond outward forms… They do not have a long enough range to penetrate the depths of the inward nature of things.'

chunks.title: 'Ali's letter to Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr (Letter 27), quoting the Prophet: 'I do not fear for my community from the believer or the unbeliever
chunks.text: 'Ali's letter to Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr (Letter 27), quoting the Prophet: 'I do not fear for my community from the believer or the unbeliever. As for the believer, Allah will protect him because of his belief, and, as for the unbeliever, Allah will humiliate him because of his unbelief. But I fear about every one of you who is a hypocrite in his heart and learned in speech. He speaks what you can accept, but he does what you cannot accept.'

chunks.title: Footnote worth knowing: throughout Islamic history, every time a reformer arises and 'the interests of the unjust and the profiteers are end
chunks.text: Footnote worth knowing: throughout Islamic history, every time a reformer arises and 'the interests of the unjust and the profiteers are endangered, these latter immediately don the disguise of sanctity, and display their piety and religion.'

chunks.title: THE DECISIVE EQUATION: 'with every bit that stupidity increases, the way opens further for hypocrisy
chunks.text: THE DECISIVE EQUATION: 'with every bit that stupidity increases, the way opens further for hypocrisy. The struggle with the stupid and stupidity is the struggle with hypocrisy too, for the stupid are the tools in the hands of the hypocrites. Naturally, the struggle with the foolish and with foolishness is to disarm the hypocrites, and take the sword out of their hands.'

chunks.title: al-Ma'mun ar-Rashid — famous for epicureanism and extravagance — seeing the 'Alawis ascendant, changed clothing and appeared publicly in a n
chunks.text: al-Ma'mun ar-Rashid — famous for epicureanism and extravagance — seeing the 'Alawis ascendant, changed clothing and appeared publicly in a new light. Abu Hanifah al-Iskafi, who took nothing from him, wrote a panegyric on his worn fur coat; asked why he wore it so long, al-Ma'mun replied: 'Tales are left behind by kings among the Arabs and the non-Arabs, not by fine cotton and linen!' — i.e. cultivated austerity as image-management.

chunks.title: The general lesson: 'each in his way excelling in the well-tried and oppressive politics of “holding the Qur'an up on spears”, and defeating
chunks.text: The general lesson: 'each in his way excelling in the well-tried and oppressive politics of “holding the Qur'an up on spears”, and defeating all effort and self-sacrifice, nipping each new resurgence in the bud.' The cause is 'nothing but the ignorance and unknowing of people, which does not know how to distinguish between slogans and reality' — so reform is blocked and must start again from the beginning.

chunks.title: Not confined to any one group: wherever a group of Muslims, or people 'got up in the garb of religion', become a tool for the advance of non
chunks.text: Not confined to any one group: wherever a group of Muslims, or people 'got up in the garb of religion', become a tool for the advance of non-Muslims and of colonialism — the colonialists covering them and using them as a shield — then it becomes impossible to fight the colonialists without first dealing with the shields.

akhlaq.lesson: Learn to distinguish the Qur'an's message from the opportunistic use of Qur'anic symbols; resist manipulation by slogans that bypass understanding.

units.title: 'Ali, the True Imam and Leader

chunks.title: ⚠ Coverage note: my source text was truncated before this closing section
chunks.text: ⚠ Coverage note: my source text was truncated before this closing section. What follows is the frame the book has built toward; verify details directly in your copy.

chunks.title: The convergence of the two powers
chunks.text: The convergence of the two powers. The book's whole argument arrives here: 'Ali is the model of leadership precisely because he possessed attraction and repulsion together, each properly directed. Part 1 showed whom he drew; Part 2 showed whom he drove off; the true Imam is defined by the correctness of both.

chunks.title: The criterion restated (Ch
chunks.text: The criterion restated (Ch. 4): having both powers is not itself a virtue — Genghis Khan, Hajjaj and Mu'awiyah had both. What certifies leadership is who is attracted and who is repelled. 'Ali attracted Maytham, Ibn as-Sikkit, Sa'sa'ah, the man whose hand he amputated; he repelled the money-worshippers of Jamal, the schemers of Siffin, and the fanatics of Nahrawan.

chunks.title: Leadership requires love (Ch
chunks.text: Leadership requires love (Ch. 12): power and force drive people like sheep without awakening their inner strengths, and even justice lifelessly enforced is insufficient. The ruler must love his people like a father and possess a personality that fosters devotion — Letter 53 to Malik al-Ashtar is the charter.

chunks.title: Leadership requires repulsion (Chs
chunks.text: Leadership requires repulsion (Chs. 17–21): the same leader must be able to strike at greed, at political hypocrisy, and — hardest of all — at sincere but ignorant piety, without being disarmed by calloused foreheads and tattered shirts.

chunks.title: The demand on the follower (Ch
chunks.text: The demand on the follower (Ch. 20): 'the true Shi'ah is a copy of 'Ali's conduct; the Shi'ah must also, like 'Ali, have two sides to his character' — and the Foreword's question returns: do we attract and repel the same people he did?

akhlaq.lesson: Let leadership be anchored in truth, justice, courage, and service so that attraction and repulsion become expressions of a coherent moral life.
